articles.title: Russell Brand and the ‘blokeification’ of Christianity
articles.author: Jonathan Abernethy-Barkley, Lecturer in Theology and Religious Studies, King's College London
paras: When Russell Brand was sentenced to ten years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault in November 2026, a peculiar image stood out: his rosary.
Various news outlets reported that Brand was using a rosary during his sentencing. Reporters even caught sight of a crucifix through the window of the prison van that transported him.

As both a sociologist of religion and an ordained minister, I am not necessarily preoccupied with whether Brand is a sincere Christian. Instead, I am interested in what this public display of faith says about the shifting links between religion, masculinity and celebrity culture. This has led me to look into what I call the “blokeification” of Christianity. Something that will be explored further in my forthcoming book, Global Awakenings Populism, Conspirituality & Conversion Narratives.

In a British context, I would describe the “blokeification” of Christianity as an attempt to reshape Christian faith and religious identity through a masculine, often laddish, lens. It’s a move that pushes back against the idea that church is excessively formal, sentimental, or feminine.

In recent years, I have seen this in churches where religious belief is discussed over a pint in a pub, where football and “banter” build community, and where leaders try to present themselves as ordinary, relatable blokes. There is nothing inherently wrong with making church more relatable for men, but it is worth questioning the particular kind of masculinity it projects.

This is especially obvious in certain online Christian circles where faith starts to merge with gym culture, self-improvement and established gender roles. While many churches and religious groups are working to push back against the kind of masculinity promoted by personalities such as Andrew Tate, is equally important to examine how Christianity itself might be building and promoting its own specific masculine ideals.

At the same time, even if they aren’t coming from the same religious groups, more populist and far-right movements are appropriating Christian symbols. In these spaces, Christianity becomes less about actual belief or practice and more about cultural identity, nationalism and masculine strength.
Muscular Christianity and blokeification

In the UK, you could argue that the roots of this go back to the muscular Christianity movement of the mid-Victorian era. Starting in the 1850s, several clergymen and educators felt that Christianity had become too passive, domestic and disconnected from men’s lives.

Through writers like Charles Kingsley and Thomas Hughes, they pushed to reclaim – or “blokeify” – Christianity by focusing on physical strength and moral character. This played out in the growing connection between Christianity and organised sports. In fact, many of Britain’s most famous football clubs (including Manchester City, Aston Villa and Bolton Wanderers) started as church teams in the late 1800s.

Similar ideals can be found in the Boys Brigade, which combined religious teaching with military-style drills, and in the Young Men’s Christan Association (the YMCA), founded in London in 1844, which combined physical strength, moral worldview formation and shared community experiences.

The core strategy of such movements hasn’t changed much: take the secular spaces where men already hang out and fill them with Christian meaning. While the Victorians used rugby pitches and boxing rings to show that a man could be both tough and devout, modern blokeified Christianity uses pubs, five-a-side football, gyms and podcasts to do the same thing.
This brings us back to Russell Brand and how he fits within these wider sociological trends in religion.

The public presentation of Brand’s coming to faith appeared less concerned with a Damascene encounter (a sudden and transformative religious experience, akin to St Paul’s conversion on the road to Damascus), and more with a rugged, performative expression of Christianity, laden with celebrity culture. Brand’s media-friendly baptism in the River Thames, stripped to the waist and wearing swimming shorts, was presided over not by an ordained minister but by celebrity adventurer Bear Grylls. Brand would later replicate the ritual for another convert, this time wearing water-drenched white briefs.
Responding to the backlash, Brand remarked: “It might seem a bit soon to be baptising people, but the Apostles did it on day one, so here we are.”

In aligning his expressions of faith with the manosphere, Brand followed an increasingly well-trodden path among influencers and conspiracy theorists, drawing on Christian rhetoric to legitimise and market their particular interpretations of the world.
Then, there is the question of style over substance. Brand was pictured carrying a Bible to court, and even released a step-by-step guide to becoming a Christian in seven days.

But his apparent difficulty recalling or accurately quoting scripture during interviews raises questions about the relationship between the public performance of Christianity and the slower, less glamorous process of religious formation.

While Brand’s flashier moments of conversion have dominated the headlines, the quieter work of faith – and the real test of character – usually plays out away from the spotlight. Seen through that lens, Brand’s public turn to religion is less a standalone curiosity than a mirror of how masculinity and celebrity culture are reshaping faith today.

articles.title: Behind the joy of Marc Chagall’s circus art is a story of loss and exile
articles.author: Lauren Warner-Treloar, PhD Candidate, Art and Design History, Kingston University
paras: For most visitors, the circus is a place to escape reality, but for Marc Chagall, it was a way to hold on to it. Marc Chagall: The Circus at the Hepworth Wakefield reveals how the artist turned childhood memories of travelling performers into a lifeline through migration, war and loss.

Chagall first encountered travelling circus performers in Vitebsk (then part of the Russian empire, now Belarus), where he was born into a Jewish family in 1887. Chagall spent most of his adult life outside Vitebsk, living in France, Germany and later the United States. Chagall and his wife Bella sought refuge in the US following the German invasion of France in May 1940.

He had become a French citizen in 1937 at the age of 50 as Europe descended into antisemitism and war. But thanks to Alfred H. Barr Jr, the first director of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and the Emergency Rescue Committee, the Chagalls were able to flee to New York in 1941.

Marc Chagall: The Circus argues that the circus became a visual language through which Chagall carried memories of his hometown across decades of movement and exile. It persuasively shows how the performers, animals and spectacles became recurring motifs that Chagall revisited time and again as he navigated life abroad.
Despite the jocularity of the circus imagery in Chagall’s work, the exhibition is really about the relationship between performance and identity, as well as the precarity of modern life.

Curator Eleanor Clayton told me she was struck by “how much his childhood memories of travelling circus performers remained a vivid reference for his works”. She noted that: “Chagall would later remark that these recurring symbols functioned as a visual vocabulary, like a poet uses words, nonetheless creating new poems each time.”

The exhibition devotes an entire room to Chagall’s Cirque, a suite of colour and black and white lithograph prints created in 1967. Commissioned as an artist’s book by the French publisher Tériade, Cirque is represented through both its lithographs and accompanying text.

The display of lithographs, enhanced by the first full English translation of Chagall’s 1967 essay Cirque, reveals how singular Chagall’s focus was on certain figures and motifs. By viewing the lithographs together, viewers can readily see the importance of continuity in exile for Chagall as he returned to these figures and motifs across many years.

The perspective in these lithographs is often from above, looking down. Certain figures appear throughout, such as a fiddler, a red horse and a performer in a pointy hat. Countless tiny, faceless people line the circus ring from top to bottom while the performers are magnified as they float through the space of the circus ring. The effect is dreamlike, yet oddly familiar, as though viewers are glimpsing remembered fragments.
One of the most revealing works in the suite is Circus (Mourlot 500) because it brings these elements together into a single composition.

Slightly above the centre of the image, a couple on a trapeze poses with what appears to be a red, green and white horse with a yellow mane. The upper figure is yellow and seems to hold the second figure, a woman who is depicted mostly in white with some pink highlights. Far below them is a bright yellow circus ring, where a yellow-hued performer in a pointy hat lunges away from them, clasping a bouquet of white flowers in one hand while looking back over his shoulder.

They all seem to occupy a space between performance and dream. The work recalls Chagall’s repeated depictions of himself and his wife Bella, who died during their American exile, turning a circus performance into a kind of reunion instead.

In contrast with this lithograph is a painting, on loan from Tate, “The Dance and the Circus” (1950). Here the viewpoint shifts below the action, looking up at the flying figures of a fiddler rendered as a red cow, with the couple reappearing on the far left. A young girl painted in shades of green and blue lunges towards the fiddler and couple, thrusting a bouquet at them with a slight smile on her lips.
The entire painting is infused with yellow. The recurring elements are present, but recollection and performance are more closely entwined.

The painting opens outwards, while the lithograph appears enclosed in its depiction. This suggests that for Chagall, the circus was an imaginative space where memories and relationships could be projected indefinitely.
The exhibition’s greatest strength is how it shows the persistence of these motifs over the decades.

It highlights how the circus served as a space where Chagall could continuously revisit and rework themes of memory, family and loss. However, on occasion, the focus on universal themes risks downplaying the specific historical Jewish and eastern European contexts underpinning these images.

The recurring figures, animals and symbolic characters point towards the vanished world that continued to influence Chagall’s imagination. Chagall’s life and career moved across national borders, but the exhibition overall reminds viewers how deeply rooted his imagination and practice remained in the Jewish culture of eastern Europe.

For Chagall, the circus was a means of preserving memory when his home had become inaccessible to him. The exhibition’s achievement lies in showing how Chagall used the circus motif as an imaginative space to which he could return when the world that had shaped him could no longer be recovered.
Marc Chagall: The Circus is at The Hepworth Wakefield until 25 April 2027

articles.title: Half a million books are going into UK prisons – but there are still barriers to reading that need to be tackled
articles.author: Caroline Cauchi, Reader in Creative Writing, University of Hull
paras: For people in prison, reading can build confidence, provide a sense of achievement, offer imaginative escape and help maintain connections with family, other prisoners and the wider world.

In November 2026, half a million books were distributed across UK prisons in an ambitious initiative led by The Reading Agency. The programme comes towards the end the National Year of Reading 2026, a campaign to encourage people across the UK to rediscover reading for pleasure and make it part of everyday life.
It is a remarkable investment in reading. But getting books into prisons is only part of the challenge. How do we ensure people have the confidence, opportunity and choice to read them?

Our research has found that how people see themselves as readers can shape their engagement with books. If reading for pleasure is to become a lasting part of prison life, we need to understand these barriers and offer different ways to overcome them.

In focus groups with people in prison, we encountered complicated relationships with reading. Some participants were interested in books but lacked confidence in their abilities. Others struggled to see themselves as readers at all. Reading aloud or discussing a text in front of others could feel exposing, particularly for those uncertain about their skills.

The prison environment presents further challenges. Restricted movement, institutional routines and limited access to libraries can leave people with little control over what, when and how they read. An interest in books does not always translate into an opportunity to engage with them.

Group discussions and author visits can be valuable, but not everyone feels comfortable participating nor has permission to attend. For some, the freedom to read privately, reflect without scrutiny and progress at their own pace may be just as important.
Bringing the book club into the cell
These findings informed the development of the University of Hull’s digital book club for readers and writers, launched earlier this year.

Delivered through in-cell technology that is available in more than 90 prisons across England and Wales, the book club is accessed via secure laptops. These allow prisoners to access preloaded reading materials and activities in their cells without requiring internet access, and offers an alternative to organised reading activities.

We designed guided reading and creative writing exercises at beginner, intermediate and advanced levels. Questions invite readers to explore characters’ decisions, consider different perspectives and develop their own interpretations. Creative exercises encourage them to imagine alternative storylines or draw connections with their own experiences, without requiring personal disclosure.

Participation is voluntary for prisoners. Those who complete and submit their activities can receive a University of Hull certificate, offering recognition that may be meaningful for people who lack confidence in their reading and writing abilities.

The aim is not simply to provide electronic texts, but to create opportunities for independent literary engagement, reflection and creative expression. Readers can participate privately, without the pressure of a classroom or group discussion.
Why contemporary books matter

Developing the digital book club also raised another question: what books could people actually read? Choice matters, and reading for pleasure involves discovering different authors, genres and stories, including contemporary literature.

We wanted to move beyond the titles already in the public domain. So we approached The Reading Agency with a proposal to make its Quick Reads titles – which were already available digitally through our existing book club – free to people in prison.

Unbeknown to us, the charity was already planning a major initiative to mark 20 years of Quick Reads. Nearly half a million copies of 11 titles were to be distributed across UK prisons, supported by author events, workshops and National Prison Radio activities. The programme also had the backing of author Lee Child, the UK’s first prison reading laureate.

Digital provision was not originally part of its plans, but The Reading Agency welcomed our proposal. As a result, four of the 11 Quick Reads in Prison titles are now available as ebooks, including one by Child, accompanied by our guided reading and creative writing activities.
This was made possible through the charity’s willingness to embrace the proposal and the agreement of authors and publishers to license their work for secure digital use.

What began as a University of Hull project has now become a new element of a national reading initiative, demonstrating how research, reading organisations and the publishing industry can work together to widen access to contemporary literature.
The next chapter belongs to publishers

The four Quick Reads titles have been licensed for digital access for just six months. This is an important start, but it raises a wider question: why should access to contemporary literature in prisons be exceptional rather than commonplace?

We believe that books should not be a privilege to be earned, or reading an opportunity dependent on institutional routines. People in prison should be able to discover and enjoy literature as part of everyday life.

Digital books can help make this possible. They cannot replace physical books, libraries, reading groups or author visits, nor should they. Each offers something different. But in-cell access can reach people who might otherwise struggle to participate, allowing them to read independently and at a time that suits them.

Now publishers now have an opportunity to build on this progress by making more titles available for secure digital use and supporting longer licensing periods. Four titles and a six-month licence should be the beginning, not the limit of our ambition.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a huge cultural moment – it’s time to stop asking if video games are art
articles.author: Garry Crawford, Professor of Cultural Sociology, University of Salford
paras: On November 10 2026, PlayStation and Xbox owners across the UK began downloading a 212GB file. Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) would not come out until November 19, but the pre-load alone broke Virgin Media O2’s records for peak traffic and daily data volume.
In December 2023, GTA VI’s first trailer drew more than 93 million views in 24 hours, a YouTube record for a non-music video. In May 2025 the second trailer exceeded 475 million views in a day.

But one of the most telling signs of the game’s cross-cultural reach comes from basketball. On November 18, the eve of GTA VI’s release, the Miami Heat basketball team hosted the Milwaukee Bucks in a regular NBA game the club billed as “A Night in Vice City”.

Vice City is Grand Theft Auto’s fictional version of Miami, and for one night the Heat basketball team existed in that world. The players wore Vice City kit and fans were able to snack at Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell, the game’s fictional fast-food chains.

Between 2018 and 2021, the Heat’s “Vice” jerseys paid tribute to the 1980s TV drama Miami Vice. This time around the reference point is a video game. It is clear that video games are no longer simply covered by other culture – they are actively reshaping it.
This article is part of our State of the Arts series. These articles tackle the challenges of the arts and heritage industry – and celebrate the wins, too.

But it wasn’t always like this. In our forthcoming book, Consuming Video Games, fellow sociologist Tom Brock and I trace how video games began as experiments in military-funded research labs, then moved into bars and arcades alongside jukeboxes and pinball machines.

These were largely the haunts of young men, and jukeboxes and pinball carried an air of youthful rebellion as a form of leisure that felt distinct from adult respectability. Arcade games took that image with them when consoles and home computers brought them into living rooms and bedrooms. Parents, teachers and commentators dismissed them as a frivolous distraction, or simply a passing craze.
My colleagues and I argue that games have been held back by a particular stereotype of young, geeky, possibly toxic masculinity. That stereotype was not without foundation.

For decades, games were marketed mostly at boys and young men. Women who played, made or wrote about games sometimes faced abuse. This was most visible during the 2014 GamerGate campaign that saw an orchestrated barrage of online abuse against women in gaming. But the behaviour of a vocal minority came to stand in for the medium as a whole, and our research with women in the industry and in gaming communities suggests that while there is still work to do, the culture is far broader than the stereotype allows.
Yet the old image lingers. One survey from our research suggests people still place video games alongside reality TV, tattoos and shopping malls as having no cultural value at all.

Shut out of respectable culture, gaming built its own. Players “copied and swapped game tapes, traded tips in playgrounds, and read magazines”, while specialist magazines and TV programmes taught people how to talk about games. Games are now played, but also watched, discussed, performed, collected, mourned and lived.
The scale is no longer in question. More than half of British adults play video games, yet popularity is not the same as respect.

Writing in the Guardian’s gaming culture newsletter, Pushing Buttons, Keith Stuart predicted that coverage of GTA VI would follow “a familiar pattern”, with reviewers admitting they haven’t played a game since Pac-Man, “in a way they never would while discussing any other art form”. Jamie Sefton, managing director of the northern games network Game Republic, said he remains baffled “as to why games are still not covered extensively in mainstream media”.

Much in the same way film came to be taken seriously as art, legitimacy rarely comes from inside a culture. It is granted by outsiders who already hold cultural authority: critics, curators, broadcasters and funders.

Even then, only certain games are seen as having artistic merit, usually smaller independent ones such as Journey (2012) or Disco Elysium (2019). Blockbusters such as Call of Duty (2003) rarely, if ever, are. This splits games into a handful of worthy games and the rest, which does little for the medium as a whole.

GTA VI sits firmly in “the rest”. It is loud, commercial, violent and controversial, the kind of game that cultural gatekeepers have learned to dismiss. But in August 2026, Netflix premiered the GTA VI preview where it recorded 31.1 million views in four days and ranked top of the platform’s English-language film chart. A few months later, an NBA team dipped into the world of Vice City. These are exactly the kind of “outsiders” that can shift how a medium is seen.

Film, television and pop music all made the journey from dismissed to respected, and it is tempting to ask when games will follow. But asking whether games are art is possibly the wrong question. What matters is the place they already hold in people’s lives – and that broadcasters, sports clubs and others outside gaming are starting to take note.

articles.title: Sewing an infinity of phalluses – how Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama confronted the male-dominated art world by mocking it
articles.author: Midori Yamamura, Associate Professor of Art History, City University of New York
paras: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama’s installations are big, bold and controversial. From the time she burst upon the pop art scene in the 1960s until her death on Aug. 14, 2026, at the age of 97, she challenged the Western, male-dominated art world. She also upended assumptions about mental disorders, which many people have uncritically seen as the source of her creativity. Her phallic sculptures and confounding mirror rooms are still popular, and they defy artistic classifications.
Kusama’s resistance to categorization raises an intriguing question: What is her lasting effect on the art world?

Kusama took a major step into the global art scene after sending two canvases for display at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum on Feb. 5, 1962. After that, she shifted her direction to avant-garde sculpture. She created Accumulation No. 1, her first work in a series that employed sewn phallic protrusions. The series thrust her into New York City’s pop art scene and would lead to her fantastical Infinity Mirror Rooms installation.
A major retrospective of her work is on view at the Stedelijk Museum through Jan. 17, 2027.

The specter of her mental health issues, however, still undermines her art’s significance. Critics often link the repetition in her work to obsessive-compulsive disorder. But as an art historian who has studied Kusama extensively, I argue that she intentionally used compulsivity to examine gender issues in the art world. A close look at Accumulation No. 1 reveals how she pulled this off.

Kusama’s emphasis on gender came into focus when she arrived in the male-dominated New York art world. During the 1940s and 50s, while abstract expressionism reigned in New York, women in the scene were treated as wives and assistants.

Painter Grace Hartigan had to adopt the pseudonym “George” to gain recognition. By the 1960s, that was starting to change. Venezuelan sculptor Marisol Escobar’s May 1962 exhibition at the Stable Gallery bucked the trend of gender conformity by integrating self-portraits into her sculpture series.

Kusama’s Accumulation No. 1 emerged as New York artists were seeking to move beyond abstract expressionism. The gestural paintings of this art movement were what some critics saw as an existential struggle toward originality coded as masculine. Pop artists refused this model: They turned instead to ready-made objects and impersonal repetition, evoking factory production.

Kusama procured furniture and egg cartons for her Accumulation sculptures, as well as a wooden rowboat for another sculpture that became Aggregation One Thousand Boats Show. She decided to focus on sewing — an art rooted in her female Japanese education — and she ordered a sewing machine.

Kusama embraced femininity by using phalluses – a symbol of patriarchal authority – made from assorted fabrics sewn into tubular shapes, filled with cotton and painted white. She upholstered an armchair with these protrusions, colonizing an eerie domestic scene with phalluses made through a traditionally feminine craft.
In this way, she transformed furniture into a vessel of complex meaning, with gender as the key component to interpretation.

Art critics and scholars have often interpreted the time-consuming process of creating these phalluses as evidence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis. But this assumption overshadows Kusama’s careful planning and deliberate choices in her art. Intensive manual labor is a common component of Kusama’s work.

In 2008, filmmaker Heather Lenz interviewed Kusama’s friend Helen Yrissary, who helped sew the protrusions on the armchair. She noted that while there were always five assistants who crafted the phalluses, only Kusama herself secured them to the chair. In Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, obsession was more of a calculated aesthetic and conceptual choice than a compulsive action.

Kusama knew about obsessive-compulsive disorder and the anxiety it can cause. Drawing on Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories, she explained in her autobiography that she developed the phallic image while she was exploring “kyōfu” – fear, or feelings of the uncanny – in the Accumulation series. According to Freud, the potential for the uncanny is rooted in a child’s first awareness of the anatomical differences between the sexes. He postulated that female children are traumatized when they realize they lack a penis, creating what he called penis envy.
Kusama’s Accumulation series may have functioned as a satire of penis envy. And it may have led her to the idea of vanquishing men’s authoritative power.

In one of her self-portraits from 1966, Kusama flaunted a phallic protrusion near her crotch. This gesture suggests that the protrusion might be her own penis, that she might be bisexual or that she might not fall under the category of “female.” Such efforts to redefine female sexuality inspired many female artists at the time. Toward the late 1960s, artist Louise Bourgeois, who admired Kusama’s work, created several sculptures, including Fillette (Little Girl), that employed phallic shapes as commentary on psychological complexes and gender.

But when Kusama premiered Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, The New York Times gave her work only a brief mention. When, three months later, sculptor Claes Oldenburg showed his similarly sewn “metamorphic” sculptures, he received rave reviews in numerous art magazines, bringing him to the attention of the international art world. It was only much later in the 2010s, after Kusama gained global prominence, that Oldenburg admitted her influence on his work.

Kusama’s popularity today stems from works that are both visually expansive and socially subversive. Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show was her first all-over exhibit – an exhibition in which a repeated motif covers the gallery’s four walls, drawing the audience into the work rather than asking them to view it as a separate object. On display at the Gertrude Stein Gallery from December 1963 to January 1964, it featured a sculpture of the phallus-embedded boat surrounded by its image repeating across the wall.

Although Kusama sought to subvert male authority, she appears nude in a photograph of the phallus boat installation, her back to the camera, trapped between the real and the illusory. Rowing the boat seems like the only way to escape the omnipresence of masculinity.
She seemed even more entrapped by patriarchal symbolism in her Infinity Mirror Room — Phalli’s Field, where she lays among an array of phalluses covered in red polka dots.

In 1966, Kusama found a way to break away from male domination through her “Peep Show” at the Castellane Gallery in New York. In it, she reduced the towering phallus to a small dot of light. It was her first work of psychedelic art, a category the curator Christoph Grunenberg characterized as both “artistic experiment and dissenting politics.”

Incorporating Beatles music, flickering strobe lights and mirror reflections, “Peep Show” was intended to produce effects similar to those of psychoactive drugs such as mescaline, psilocybin and LSD, liberating users from established social norms and opening the possibility of alternative values. The exhibit, later known as “Love Forever,” also aimed to alter perception by inducing synesthesia — a neurological state in which stimulating one sensory-cognitive pathway triggers involuntary experiences in another.

Kusama remembered attending a lecture by Timothy Leary, a former Harvard University psychology professor and psychedelics advocate, at the Village Theater in New York, a hub of psychedelic culture. In 1968, she collaborated with light artist Joshua White on Self-Obliteration, a fusion of sound, lights and images that Leary claimed “would demonstrate what an LSD session is like.”

Kusama’s ability to transform any neurosis she may have had into liberation began with Accumulation No. 1 and continued through Fireflies on the Water (2002), Soul Under the Moon (2002), Infinity Mirror Room—Aftermath of Obliteration of Eternity (2009) and Infinity Mirrored Room—The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away (2013). The ethereal visions embodied in her psychedelic mirror rooms stand in for the mind-altering drugs that release people from the rationality of society and fuel the desire to change.

Through Kusama’s Accumulation and Infinity Mirror Room series, I argue that she turned the human body into what philosopher Herbert Marcuse described as “an instrument of pleasure.” By making the body an instrument of pleasure rather than labor, Kusama subverted the age-old patriarchal order.

articles.title: Eminem and Damien Hirst collaboration shows the relationship between art and music is alive and well
articles.author: Glenn Fosbraey, Associate Dean of Humanities and Social Sciences, University of Winchester
paras: Few of even Eminem’s staunchest fans would have expected the rapper to find a home in a fine art gallery. Yet in 2026, when truth is often stranger than fiction, what was once inconceivable became a reality.

American Dream was a collaboration between the rapper and the artist Damien Hirst consisting of paintings and installations inspired by Eminem’s album covers. It was recently on display at London’s HENI gallery.

For centuries, western tradition has placed the visual arts at the top of an intellectual ladder, treating sight and sound as separate domains. Today however, artists, curators and researchers are increasingly interested in how our senses of sight and sound overlap, interact and enrich one another.

As a researcher of music, I find the combination of visual art and music to be one of the most fascinating pairings. At their core, the two art forms may be distinct forms of human expression, but they are deeply connected by how their use of space, rhythm and movement can express emotional responses and experiences for their viewers, listeners, or even the creators themselves.
Indeed, the two go together so well that they can be found sitting together on millions of shelves in millions of homes all over the world.

Ever since 1938, when graphic designer Alex Steinweiss created the first illustrated 78rpm record album cover (Smash Song Hits by Rodgers & Hart, which featured the songwriters’ names in lights on a shimmering marquee) popular music and visual art have been inseparable.

In his 2008 book A Brief History of Album Covers, author Jason Draper observed that some album covers are genuine pieces of high-class art that should be revered as much as the music. He cites The Beatles’ Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, Sex Pistols’ Never Mind the Bollocks and Cindi Lauper’s She’s So Unusual as examples.

Perhaps due to its ability to reach vast audiences, the medium has appealed to several revered visual artists over the years. Andy Warhol, Peter Blake, Banksy and Takashi Murakami have all created cover art across a range of musical genres.

In my new book Reading Eminem, I explain that the album format has always been Eminem’s primary form of expression. The artwork found on his front and back covers, booklets and tray inserts has been a significant part of that.

From the grotesque cartoon imagery of 1999’s The Slim Shady LP through to the “body bag” image on 2024’s The Death of Slim Shady (Coup de Grâce), Eminem has used visuals art as a way to enhance the stories and characters contained within the songs themselves.
With 2004’s Encore CD booklet photographs, Eminem has even provided fans with an additional narrative, appearing to shoot at his audience at the end of a performance.

In recent years, the humble album cover has even been deemed worthy of promotion to art gallery status. Exhibitions such as For the Record: Photography & the Art of the Album Cover at The Photographers’ Gallery, London, Art & Vinyl at Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco and Playback: Art Of The Album Sleeve at Lincoln Castle have underscored the medium as a serious artform.

In 2022, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art collaborated with Interscope, commemorating the label’s 30th anniversary by displaying reinterpretations of Interscope album art from an intergenerational group of visual artists. Among them was Hirst, who re-imagined album covers from Eminem’s discography based on their themes and lyricism.

Described by the HENI gallery as “a landmark collaboration that unites two of the most influential forces in contemporary art and music”, the show American Dream combined Hirst’s trippy interpretations of 12 Eminem album covers with a series of pharmaceutical-themed installations and visual motifs inspired by the rapper’s lyrics.

On the face of it, the exhibition may not have offered anything ground-breaking. But the fact that album covers, once considered part of a “low” culture medium, are being displayed in settings previously reserved for highbrow cultural capital is significant. I for one hope this trend continues.

articles.title: Why are people listening to train journeys to fall asleep?
articles.author: Chloe Harrison, Senior Lecturer in Stylistics, Aston University
paras: It’s a dark and rainy evening and you’re settled into a comfy seat in a warm, quiet and dimly lit train carriage. You lean your head against the soft back of the chair and hear the rain fall against the window while you watch the hills rolling by. If there is something about this experience that sounds relaxing to you, then you’re not alone.

Sleep stories on meditation apps revive one of humanity’s oldest practices, bedtime storytelling, and repackage it for the digital age. Since their introduction on the meditation app Calm, they have been listened to more than 1 billion times. At a time when many adults struggle to fall or stay asleep, their popularity suggests a growing interest in stories that offer something different from conventional narratives.

One of the most popular forms of sleep story is the train genre, which features scenic rail journeys through a variety of real and fictional landscapes around the world. You could travel through Johannesburg in Africa, Darjeeling in Asia and Switzerland in Europe or even take a magical ride on the North Pole’s Christmas Express.

Some of the most famous stories set on trains feature action, murder and mystery, often requiring a bit of detective work from the reader. Think Murder on the Orient Express by Agatha Christie (1934) or Strangers on a Train by Patricia Highsmith (1950). The train-themed sleep stories in Calm’s library are very different. These audio narratives contain no conflict, suspense or adversary. They are designed to be engaging – but not so engaging that listeners will still be awake to hear the ending.

The train journey is particularly well suited to this purpose. Its steady movement along a predetermined route transforms falling asleep into a journey in which the listener can relinquish control and simply be carried towards their destination.

A study of train sleep stories I worked on with Paula Ghintuialǎ, an expert in how style in language and screen media shapes interpretation, explores the recurring linguistic features and storytelling choices that make these narratives unique, and which encourage sleep. Understanding how these unusual stories work offers an opportunity to rethink the linguistic and narrative strategies through which stories both hold, and deliberately release, our attention.

Each story is structured around the same metaphor: sleep as a journey. The listener becomes the traveller, relaxation becomes movement along the route and sleep becomes the destination. Importantly, the journey is smooth and stress-free. Trains run on time, the seat is comfortable and spacious, and fellow passengers are few and quiet.

Every story also has a narrator who becomes your travelling companion. First, they give instructions for relaxing. You are told to “take in a few long deep breaths”, to “close your eyes” and to “let the weight of your body sink comfortably into your bed”. Similar to guided meditation practices, you are addressed through direct second-person (“you”) to help focus your attention on your immediate physical or physiological experience.
Gradually, you become a character inside the story. The narrator continues their instructions asking you to “imagine” or “picture” yourself, to shift your focus to another time and place.

Through these invitations, listeners are encouraged to inhabit the perspective of a fictionalised character who embarks on a journey. Instead of thinking about tomorrow’s meeting or an unfinished email, you’re crossing the Scottish Highlands or travelling through the Alps. These characters are generic and simply described, in order to make this embodiment a more effortless experience.

Another key feature of these stories is that you don’t have to exert a lot of energy, nor do any active decision-making. Your actions take place within the confines of the train and are performed in the simple present – “you enter”, “you walk through”, “you come to”. This creates a perpetual “now”, similar to the language of mindfulness and guided imagery. These actions are also often low-energy, and paired with moments of reflection or reception. For instance, you are told that you “look”, “watch” or “see” and “notice”, “think” or “remember”.

In contrast, verbs describing the train’s movements are dynamic and incomplete (“running”, “passing”, “rolling”, “crossing”). Taken together, these patterns suggest continuous movement along a pre-set path, and establish a sense of ongoing, ambient motion. In other words, the train does the travelling for you. The route has already been decided, so all you have to do is be carried along it.

Finally, at the end of the journey, you’re described as disembarking the train, reaching a hotel room and settling into a bed. In these closing moments, the narration reconnects the fictional journey with the listener’s physical position. You might be told, for instance, that you climb into the wide bed, savouring the clean, pressed linen. The train, meanwhile, continues without you. You are asked to imagine it receding into the distance, while the end point of your own metaphorical journey – the destination of sleep – has been reached.

articles.title: Ghost Town: a dream-like film about a Japanese community haunted by the 2011 tsunami
articles.author: Bethan Michael-Fox, Senior Lecturer in English and Creative Writing, The Open University
paras: In the aftermath of the 2011 earthquake that triggered a devastating 40-metre tsunami along Japan’s Pacific coast, taxi drivers in the Iwate port town of Kamaishi started reporting strange happenings.

Several drivers described picking up passengers who vanished during their journeys. The taxi community began to refer to them as “ghost fares”. The phenomenon soon attracted attention of news outlets, and even academics. Now these ghost fares are the subject of an equally strange film called Ghost Town, directed by British documentary maker Katherine Round.

The wall of water precipitated by the 9.0 magnitude earthquake on March 11 meant that casualties were almost entirely from coastal areas, mainly Fukushima, Miyagi and Iwate. Almost 20,000 people were killed and another 2,500 were reported missing.

I first came across these stories of ghost fares while working on my PhD, which focused on cultural engagement with dying and death. In a 2014 article Richard Lloyd Parry, the Tokyo-based Asia editor of The Times, wrote:

A cab driver in the city of Sendai picked up a sad-faced man who asked to be taken to an address that no longer existed. Halfway through the journey, he looked into his mirror to see that the rear seat was empty. He drove on anyway, stopped in front of the levelled foundations of a destroyed house, and politely opened the door to allow the invisible passenger out at his former home.

Round came across the phenomenon following a devastating loss of her own. Known for her deeply humane documentaries that follow the lives of ordinary people, she flew to Japan, where she rigged the cabs of four Kaimishi taxi drivers with cameras, and invited local residents to take a ride. Round describes her film as “an enquiry into memory, myth, life and death”.

The film follows four drivers – Konno, Iwasaki, Goto and Koike – mostly at night, as they weave their way through the streets “picking up occasional passengers and conversing with a visitor to the town about their lives”.
Rather than a documentary with an obvious narrative arc, Ghost Town is, as the director describes, a film that explores “a liminal space between documentary and dream”.

Audiences feel as if they, like the passengers of the taxis, are between one place and another, witnessing what passes by. With large stretches of silence and frequent changes of location between taxis, the audience is taken on a journey over the course of one night, moving ghost-like between different spaces and places and overhearing a range of conversations.

Journalist and filmmaker Shiori Ito – whose Black Box Diaries unleashed Japan’s Me Too movement – was part of the team, working with the people of Kamaishi to help create an inclusive process that locals could feel involved in. Once filming was underway, Ito also became a part of the film itself, taking on the role of one of the taxi passengers giving an outsider’s perspective.

The film has a moving, hypnotic quietness, but it’s never actually quiet. When the driver and passenger aren’t talking, the vehicle itself seems to take over: the hum of its electric engine becomes more pronounced as it glides through deserted streets; the radio seems to get louder; and the repetitive ticking of indicators becomes rhythmic and mesmerising. Outside there is a melancholy stillness to the darkness, punctuated by the pooled light from streetlamps.

For Round, the taxi became a “mobile confession booth”, with drivers and passengers sharing spontaneous stories about their experiences and memories, their lives, fears, hopes and regrets. While we know the drivers are real, we never quite know for sure if the person making the journey is real or an actor. The truth is never explained.

In this way the ambiguity plays on the idea of the ghost fares. These passengers could just as easily be imagined or, in effect, the ghost passengers that Kamaishi taxi drivers maintained they picked up after the tsunami.

Like Iranian director Jafar Panah’s film Taxi Tehran (2015), the technique of using cameras inside a car allows for a unique perspective on a location, seeing it pass by through windows as drivers and passengers look out, ask questions and share thoughts.

In Kamaishi, one driver mentions a “a phone box filled with spirits” trying to get through. It reminded me of another Japanese phenomenon, the “wind phone”: a disconnected phone box that gives the living a place to speak with the dead and express their grief.

In an episode of The Death Studies Podcast disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope talks about how surprisingly similar disasters are around the world: big, life changing, and traumatic, they offer “brutal teachings”. There is a world before the disaster, and a world after the disaster.
The Kamaishi shown in Ghost Town has been reconstructed with modern buildings and roads, but seems deserted and haunted, its communities broken, interrupted and forever changed by the tsunami.

Regular sirens and preparation drills feature in Round’s film, reminding audiences of the risk natural disasters continue to pose. One particularly striking scene shows a taxi driver enjoying a break with his sudoku, at his favourite spot overlooking the water. Even though it was an enormous column of water barrelling in from the ocean that destroyed these coastal towns, the presence of water in Ghost Town is calming and benign.

Ghost Town functions as a retelling, a document, a memory and a reminder of the many individual lives that are affected by disasters. And of the losses they produce, and the people and legacies they leave behind.

articles.title: You Can See Everything – a mind-bending odyssey that will leave you questioning what you see
articles.author: Sarah Lahm, Lecturer in Media, Communication, and Cultural Studies, University of Leeds
paras: In their self-aware documentary You Can See Everything, filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim attempt to paint a portrait of convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. The documentary initially follows the former founder and her partner, Billy Evans, in the last 34 days before Holmes’s incarceration for defrauding investors in her failed blood testing company Theranos.

Fielder and Oppenheim have been granted seemingly unfettered access to the couple’s home life. The pair claim that they are doing this because they want people to see the “real Liz”. What the filmmakers hope to get out of it, other than unprecedented access to a figure that has seized the cultural imagination, is less clear.

I have watched You Can See Everything three times, and found it every bit as genius as everybody says. The three-hour documentary is unique in its creation of layers of hyper-reality through its cinematography, editing, sound and use of reenactments.
While it feels groundbreaking, the documentary does reflect a logical combination and evolution of the styles of directors Fielder and Oppenheim.
One in front and one behind
Fielder’s previous project The Rehearsal (2022-) will prepare any viewer for the twists and turns of You Can See Everything – and perhaps even help predict some of them.

In The Rehearsal, Fielder builds elaborate simulations of “real” places in order to rehearse difficult conversations or play out potential life choices. As the stories progress, the lines between what’s real and what’s fabricated blur.

The Rehearsal began with Fielder off camera as more of a behind-the-scenes orchestrator. But as the series progress, he became a more active participant in these “rehearsals”. For instance, in one episode he helps a woman rehearse what raising a child with someone would be like. After her initial co-parenting partner drops out, Fielder steps in and quickly becomes the centre of the experiment, allowing his obsessions and anxieties to dominate the rehearsal.

The hyper-reality in You Can See Everything operates according to similar principles. As in The Rehearsal, when Fielder steps out from behind the camera, viewers start to question everything – including Fielder himself.

In contrast, Oppenheim is never in front of the camera (except for one particularly pertinent reenactment of how the project began in the second half of the film). Unlike Fielder, he never appears in his feature documentaries. Oppenheim’s directorial style is remarkable, conjuring up haunting, peculiar portrayals of people and places through saturated colours, fantastical cinematography and dreamy soundscapes.

Oppenheim’s way of telling stories with a dreamlike quality, without explaining why his subjects behave the way they do, lends itself particularly well to painting this purposefully incomplete picture of Holmes and Evans. Through his lens, the couple are imperfect beneficiaries – or victims, as they might like to add – of America’s obsession with investment in newness and in charismatic (particularly white, middle and upper class) individuals.

In the first half, this idea is captured through tight scenes of Holmes, Evans and Fielder within the confined spaces of the couple’s rented beach cottage in San Diego. Such shots, paired with a restrained use of music, establish an atmosphere that always feels hesitant and obscure.
This might be unprecedented access, but no matter how strongly Holmes insists that Fielder and Oppenheim can see everything, you feel that they – and you – really can’t.
How do you show what you can’t see?
In the second half of the film, Holmes has started her 11-year prison sentence and the storytelling becomes less straightforward.

How do you film a documentary when one of your main subjects is essentially inaccessible? Oppenheim and Fielder creatively rise to the task by layering realities onto each other through the inclusion of varying modes of storytelling, like reenactments and even reenactments within reenactments.

This layered reality can have a disorienting and almost psychedelic quality at times – even on the seemingly straight shots. One of the most striking examples is a scene of Evans working on his laptop in the kitchen. A reptile (a blue Argentine tegu) moves slowly across the table. On the other side of the room is a screen playing a life-size AI-generated video of Holmes, talking to nobody in particular.

This trippy scene is as bizarrely haunting and unnerving as some of the intense confrontations with Billy in this final section. Wide eyed and unapologetic, Billy’s small acts of seemingly controlling behaviour (like taking over the whisking of eggs in the first half) are writ larger in Holmes’s absence and tinged by his enthusiasm for conservative politics and figures like Charlie Kirk.
In these scenes it becomes clear that while Holmes might have been the draw for the directors as the perfect documentary subject, Evans turns out to be an even better one.

You Can See Everything is breathtaking cinema. While it’s not a major departure from the pair’s previous work, what’s so special about this film is the qualities they have honed. Oppenheim’s ability to make factual narratives look more fictional than many fictions and Nathan Fielder’s aptitude for slowly building layer upon layer of hyper-reality, that leaves you questioning everything you see.

articles.title: What’s behind the bedazzling mania that’s taken over high school and college campuses?
articles.author: Jessica Rose Corey, Associate Professor of the Practice in Writing and Rhetoric, Duke University
paras: The art of transforming everyday objects from drab to fab is having a moment.
Bedazzling is experiencing a quasi-revival, while a newer craft, diamond painting, has emerged as its shiny cousin.
Both crafts involve placing resin gems or crystals on everything from canvases and coasters to tumblers and tote bags.

Bedazzling was popularized by DIY rhinestone application kits like the Ronco Rhinestone and Stud Setter in the 1970s and the Bedazzler in the 1990s. But whereas those older bedazzling techniques involved using a large staplerlike device to push studs and rhinestones into fabric, today’s bedazzling and diamond painting usually rely on wax or putty-infused pens to pick up and place drills and crystals onto objects and canvases. Today, a single item could be adorned by more than 100,000 gems of more than 100 colors, requiring weeks or months to complete a project.

To me, these activities are not simply fueled by boredom or nostalgia. Instead, they reflect a desire to interact with material, tangible things, as opposed to digital devices. They serve as a mental wellness practice. And they show how productivity and value are not synonymous.
As a geriatric millennial, I’ve always loved – and been known for – my shiny attire and accessories.

But it wasn’t until my colleagues who enjoy pottery and sewing suggested that I begin crafting, particularly diamond painting, as a way to boost my well-being that I considered becoming the person creating the glitz.

The art form easily accommodates the responsibilities of motherhood: It’s something I can do at home, where I can get tips from people online rather than needing to attend evening or weekend classes. And then there’s the twinge of satisfaction I experience after hearing each “pop” of the pen separating from the placed drill.
In short, I’m obsessed. The best part? I have a daily routine that doesn’t involve striving for perfection.

Unlike my teaching and research, diamond painting requires no line on a curriculum vitae or score on an evaluation sheet. Crafting isn’t about quantifying my worth or the pressure of making myself more beautiful. Its appeal lies in prioritizing myself, the experience of tranquility and the opportunity to work with my hands.
Making the mundane a little more marvelous
My college freshmen had different reasons for picking up the art.
Many of them came to it inadvertently. While they now enjoy bedazzling to unwind and unplug, some of them told me they originally turned to the practice to decorate their high school graduation caps.

To use a trendy Gen Z term, the craft is a form of “whimsymaxxing” – a way to imbue playfulness and joy into everyday life. College newspapers around the U.S. report that young women on campus are gemming anything that can hold a rhinestone. My students tell of dorm rooms wallpapered with sparkle. When they open their bags in class, I watch them retrieve chargers, lip gloss cases and water bottles, all adorned with gems arranged in impossibly intricate patterns.
Much of the media coverage of these art forms frames them as either a consumer trend – sparkle crafts are now a multimillion-dollar industry – or a form of therapy or self-preservation.

But I think bedazzling and diamond painting represent far more than that. Despite the fact that much of the history of sparkle crafts is documented solely by retailers, I see these current iterations of craftwork as part of a long tradition of women using craft as a means of self-expression, connection, catharsis and resistance against social constraints.
Crafting, in fact, underpins many activist movements.

In the 19th century, women abolitionists formed sewing circles, where they decorated objects with abolitionist emblems. Later, suffrage banners used stirring colors and messages to rally support for women’s right to vote. In 1979, an art installation called “The Dinner Party” commemorated women’s overlooked contributions to history through a triangular table featuring 39 place settings, each with embroidered and painted decorations. More recently, the Clothesline Project conveys the collective experience of sexual violence survivors through decorated T-shirts on a clothesline.
Standing up and standing out

In a world where the message to women is either that they are too much or not enough, bringing glitz and glam into public spaces demands women be seen and rejects a “toned-down” or “minimalist” way of moving through the world. It shows that women are prioritizing themselves and taking the time – hours for most projects – to resist consumer culture in favor of making something new.

Amid the many stresses of 21st-century womanhood – from sexual violence and unequal pay to disproportionate childcare responsibilities and unrelenting beauty standards – bedazzling and diamond painting allow women to literally add a little shimmer to their lives, one gem at a time.

Still, women’s craftwork has long occupied a complicated space between conformity and nonconformity, or collective and individual interest. While often dismissed as unimportant forms of femininity and domesticity, craftwork continues to challenge the notion that women’s labor must serve others or offer practical application.

Of course, there’s a tension between embracing femininity and resisting the expectations attached to it. At the 1968 Miss America protests, women discarded makeup, bras and other symbols of conventional beauty standards.

Yet rejecting glamour altogether overlooks its potential for empowerment, experimentation, expression, enjoyment and connection. At the 2026 Ball Without Billionaires, Amazon workers embraced glamour on their own terms, creating their own extravagant fashion show as a way to protest the Met Gala taking place just a few miles away.
The distinction between conformity and resistance lies in the purpose behind the activity and who determines it.

Bedazzling is not automatically excluded from traditional expectations of femininity, nor does every rhinestoned object constitute an act of resistance. But a meaningful difference exists between aiming to meet expectations that include looking beautiful and choosing a messy, imperfect, playful and slow process that is beautiful to those who engage in it.
In other words, shine isn’t necessarily tacky, and a desire for beauty isn’t necessarily shallow.

There’s something supremely satisfying about slow progress and adding that last gem or rhinestone. After spending so much time methodically placing individual pieces, you can step away and soak in the entirety of the work in all its glistening glory.
Labeling women as not enough or too much has led women to choose more: more color, more sparkle, more visibility, more time spent on themselves for themselves.
Plus, there’s really no such thing as too much sparkle.

articles.title: Stevie Wonder’s ‘Songs in the Key of Life’ – which spread an audacious message of love – turns 50 as the Motown legend goes on tour
articles.author: Austin McCoy, Assistant Professor of History, West Virginia University
paras: Stevie Wonder aimed to answer a lofty question in his 18th studio album, “Songs in the Key of Life”: Can we solve the world’s problems with love?

Released on Sept. 28, 1976, Wonder’s long-anticipated, 21-track double album dazzled listeners and influenced generations of artists. The album bridged the socially conscious R&B, funk, jazz and rock of the early 1970s with 1980s pop music.
As a cultural historian, I view Wonder’s record not just as a touchstone in the history of U.S. popular culture, but as a reflection of the artist’s Detroit upbringing.
Wonder is celebrating the 50th anniversary of “Songs in the Key of Life” by touring over a dozen cities in Europe and the U.S.. He will perform the entire album.
Early days as a young artist

Wonder was born Stevland Judkins in Saginaw, Michigan, on May 13, 1950, to Lula Mae Hardaway and Calvin Judkins. The elder Judkins mostly found himself unemployed, hustling in the early 1950s and forcing Hardaway into sex work.
Born prematurely, Wonder developed retinopathy after receiving too much air while incubated. This left him blind.

According to “Signed, Sealed, Delivered,” a biography of Wonder published in 2010, Wonder’s mother divorced Judkins after she and her family moved to Detroit in 1954, when Wonder was 4 years old. Left to raise six kids, Hardaway found steady work at a fish market.

From an early age, Wonder attracted attention from his mother, siblings and friends for his musical gifts. He learned to play the piano, harmonica and drums by the time he was 10. And like many aspiring Black musicians, Wonder began his life of performance by singing in a church choir, at the New Corinthian Church on the West Side of the city.
“After the first service of the day, he’d hang around and come in between services and ask to play the piano … that boy could play!” recalled Kim Weston, a Motown singer.
Motown Records Founder and CEO, Berry Gordy, Jr. signed Wonder in 1961 when the artist was 11.
At the time, Gordy compared Wonder to Ray Charles. The young prodigy recorded 13 albums and 35 singles in the decade that followed.
Wonder’s musical evolution
Wonder eventually wanted to produce his own music without Motown’s direction.
Wonder’s childhood contract with Motown expired when he turned 21. This led to turbulent negotiations for a new record deal with Motown, as Wonder fought for more creative control.
Meanwhile, Wonder expanded his sound as the negotiations stalled. He experimented more with rock. He studied funk performers like Sly Stone.

After signing a new contract with Motown, Wonder embarked on one of the most exceptional periods of album recording in the history of popular music. In collaboration with music producers Malcolm Cecil and Bob Margouleff, he released four classic albums — “Music of My Mind” and “Talking Book” in 1972, “Innervisions” in 1973 and “Fulfillingness’ First Finale” in 1974.

During his tour for “Innervisions” in August 1973, Wonder got into a car accident that left him in a coma for four days. Five months after regaining consciousness, he started performing with his band Wonderlove again.
Wonder then signed a seven-year, seven-album, US$13 million contract in 1975 and began writing “Songs in the Key of Life”.
“Songs in the Key of Life” dropped in a tenuous moment not just for Motown Records, but for Detroit and the United States.

Detroit struggled economically during the 1970s, as businesses and residents continued to move out. The unemployment rate in Detroit hovered near 14% in 1975 after layoffs from the auto industry and economic crisis shook the city.

“Songs in the Key of Life” features a bevy of collaborators, from the Wonderlove band to keyboardist Greg Phillinganes, organist Ronnie Foster, harpist Dorothy Ashby and American jazz musician Herbie Hancock to the West Angeles Church of God Choir, Hare Krishna singers and members of Wonder’s family.
The synthesis of musical genres, English, Spanish and Zulu languages, and themes like love, heartbreak, regret, spirituality and religion make Wonder’s album difficult to categorize.

Wonder reminisces about his time as a “nappy-headed boy” growing up in Detroit on the cheerful and nostalgic “I Wish.” He sings about the high jinks that he and his “hoodlum friends” got into – sneaking outside, smoking cigarettes and getting into trouble at school.

Wonder grew up in Detroit’s Brewster-Douglass projects, living at 2701 Hastings, although he later lived in homes on the city’s East and West sides before Gordy bought a home for Wonder and his family in the Bagley neighborhood in 1963.
The tracks “Village Ghetto Land” and “Pastime Paradise” chronicle poor and working-class Black folks’ struggles to survive the economic crises and malaise during the 1970s in cities like Detroit.

Wonder also celebrated Black history on the album. Dedicated to Duke Ellington, who died two years before the album’s release, “Sir Duke” also pays homage to other jazz giants like Count Basie, Louis Armstrong and Ella Fitzgerald.

The song “Black Man” is a history lesson about the contributions of Black, brown, Asian and Native Americans over the country’s 200-year history – figures like abolitionist Harriet Tubman and World War I veteran Sing Kee.
In “Ngiculela – Es Una Historia – I Am Singing,” Wonder sings in Zulu, Spanish and English, which speaks to the beauty of multiculturalism.
However, I consider love the most prominent theme of “Songs in the Key of Life.”
On the grand yet slow-burning opening track “Love’s in Need of Love Today,” Wonder sings about the need for people to nurture love.
“The concept I had in mind was that for love to be effective, it has to be fed. Love by itself is hollow,” Wonder told The Wall Street Journal in 2015.

While Wonder reflects on romance and heartbreak in songs like “Knocks Me Off of My Feet” and “Ordinary Pain,” he captures the joy of new life and fatherhood on “Isn’t She Lovely,” a song celebrating the birth of his daughter Aisha Morris in 1975.

On “As,” Wonder asks whether we can describe the meaning of love through words alone. The 7-minute song shares a hopeful spiritual, cosmic and utopian message. Lyrics like “until the day the Earth start’s turnin’ right to left” and “until the day that eight times eight is four” show how love can be illogical but enduring.
In a preacher’s tone, Wonder sings about his devotion to love, through pain and struggle and the passage of time on the last verse of “As.”
50 years later, Wonder’s influence lives on
The album was popular in Detroit, despite a mixed critical reception.

Detroit Free Press staff writer Carl Arrington reported in October 1976 that “Songs in the Key of Life” sold 10,000 copies a day in the city in its first week in stores. “There are more hooks in the songs than there are at a fisherman’s convention,” he wrote.

Two of popular music’s biggest stars in the 1980s, Michael Jackson and Prince, cited “Songs in the Key of Life” as an inspiration. Many R&B and rap artists have sampled it. Coolio and L.V.’s 1995 hit “Gangsta’s Paradise”, a reinterpretation of Wonder’s “Pastime Paradise,” became one of the biggest singles in the 1990s, selling more than 3 million copies in the U.S.
On Sept. 28, 2026, Wonder dropped a four-track EP of songs recorded during those studio sessions for “Songs in the Key of Life.”

“They were part of what I was feeling and discovering as we made it,” Wonder said in a statement about the previously unreleased songs. “They bring me back to that time in my life, and now they get to become part of yours.”

articles.title: Readers of fanfiction have a lot in common with 18th- and 19th-century fiction lovers
articles.author: Amy Louise Blaney, Knowledge Exchange Coordinator, University of Wolverhampton
paras: When Archive of Our Own , the world’s largest fanfiction archive, announced that it could be unavailable for weeks following a “security incident”, many readers reacted with some distress. Across social media, fans half-jokingly talked about experiencing withdrawal symptoms and mourned interrupted reading schedules.
The reaction may seem uniquely digital. Yet, readers waiting for the return of Archive of Our Own have more in common with 18th- and 19th-century readers than they might realise.

Many fanfiction writers publish stories chapter by chapter, often releasing updates according to a regular schedule over weeks, months, or even years. This allows readers to follow narratives in real time. The result is a shared experience of suspense, discussion and speculation.
Long before online archives existed, popular fiction was also often consumed in instalments.

Improvements in printing technology, together with rising literacy rates and expanding commercial networks, enabled books, periodicals and newspapers to reach larger audiences than ever before. Books nevertheless remained relatively expensive commodities because of the costs associated with paper, printing and binding. One early solution was to issue works in instalments, or fascicles, which were separately published instalments of a book or other printed works. This approach allowed publishers to spread production costs, and the related financial risk, over time, reducing the upfront cost for readers. Whether by design or accident, serialisation also served to create a culture of anticipation as audiences waited for the next part of a story.

Serial publication is only part of the story. Some modern fanfiction communities are characterised by a high degree of interaction between writers and readers. Readers comment on chapters, speculate about future developments, offer feedback, and sometimes even influence the direction of a work as it is being written.

While the technologies are different, this kind of participatory reading culture would have been familiar to 18th- and 19th-century authors. Samuel Richardson, for example, encouraged and embraced interactions with readers, and was notoriously attentive to their reactions. Discussions with friends, admirers, and critics shaped his thinking about Pamela (1740); while reader response influenced the development of its sequel, Pamela in Her Exalted Condition (1741). Although increasingly dismissive of reader feedback as his career progressed, Richardson also revised later editions of Clarissa (1747 to 1748), altering aspects of the text in response to feedback from his readership.
Reading in the 18th century was also rarely a solitary activity. Books circulated through friendship networks, generated extension discussion among readers, and even performed texts aloud.

As an avid reader and frequent correspondent, many of Jane Austen’s surviving letters reveal the innate sociability of 18th-century literary culture. On February 9 1807, for example, she tells her sister Cassandra that “We are reading Clarentine, and are surprised to find how foolish it is. I remember liking it much less on a second reading than at the first and it does not bear a third at all.”

Her novel Northanger Abbey (published posthumously in 1817 but written earlier) offers a vivid depiction of this culture. The friendship between protagonist Catherine Morland and Isabella Thorpe is cemented through their shared enthusiasm for gothic novels, particularly the works of Ann Radcliffe. Chapter six sees the two girls avidly discussing Radcliffe’s 1794 novel The Mysteries of Udolpho, with Catherine declaring: “I am delighted with the book! I should like to spend my whole life in reading it.”
If Richardson and Austen capture the formation of literary communities, the reaction to Sherlock Holmes’s death demonstrates the power such communities could wield.

When Arthur Conan Doyle killed off his famous detective in 1893, more than 20,000 readers of the Strand magazine, which published the stories, cancelled their subscriptions and others wrote letters urging the author to reverse his decision. Long before readers could leave comments on fanfiction chapters or express their dissatisfaction with a book’s conclusion at an author signing, literary audiences were already seeking to shape the futures of the fictional worlds they loved.
Holmes’s eventual resurrection has become one of literature’s most famous examples of readers refusing to accept an author’s final word.

Richardson also dealt with his fair share of this. Lady Bradsheigh and Lady Echlin were two readers who were so deeply invested in the fate of Clarissa’s heroine that they suggested revisions and alternative endings to Richardson that would have changed her tragic fate. Although Richardson ultimately resisted such changes.
If a writer can’t be moved to make changes then readers can write their own stories.

One of the most well known tenets of fanfiction is its revisitation, revision and expansion of existing fictional worlds. Fans write alternative endings, explore paths not taken by the original author, and create sequels, prequels and parallel narratives that expand fictional worlds beyond their canonical boundaries.

Take Ali Hazelwood’s 2021 romance novel The Love Hypothesis, which was adapted from her 2018 Star Wars fanfic Head Over Feet. Originally published on Archive of Our Own under the pen name Ever-so-reylo, the story imagined an alternate universe to the Star Wars sequel trilogy (Star Wars: The Force Awakens,2015; Star Wars: The Last Jedi, 2017 and Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, 2019) in which enemies Rey and Kylo Ren (Ben Solo) become unlikely lovers.

We can see similar engagement with existing worlds in 18th-century works too. For instance, Poems Occasion’d by Reading the Travels of Captain Lemuel Gulliver (1727) was a response to Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels (1726) most commonly attributed to Alexander Pope. There was also John Kelly’s continuation of Pamela, Pamela’s Conduct in High Life (1741) and Henry Fielding’s satiric parody Shamela (1741).

So the desire to continue stories, debate characters, recommend favourite texts, or imagine alternative endings endures. What has changed is the speed with which these responses can be shared, the size of the communities that can form around them, and the number of people able to participate. Modern fanfiction is not a break with literary culture so much as the latest manifestation of some of reading culture’s oldest habits.

articles.title: Why do some people think Michelangelo’s David is gay? My research zones in on his iconic stance
articles.author: Farid Pazhoohi, Lecturer in Psychology, University of Plymouth
paras: Michelangelo’s David is one of the most celebrated representations of masculine beauty in art history. Its muscular body, imposing presence and heroic subject (the biblical giant-slayer) have made it a symbol of male strength for more than five centuries. Yet one of its most recognisable features – the way David stands – may complicate that interpretation.

David stands with most of his weight on one leg, causing his hips to tilt and his shoulders to shift in the opposite direction. This posture, known as contrapposto, was established in classical sculpture to create a more natural and dynamic representation of the human body. One famous example is Polykleitos’ Doryphoros, created around 440BC.

My colleagues and I have investigated how this particular posture influences perceptions of men. Our findings suggest that, for modern viewers, it can make male figures appear less masculine, less dominant and more likely to be perceived as non-heterosexual.

We created digitally manipulated versions of classical statues, including David, varying the degree of contrapposto while keeping other characteristics constant. We conducted three experiments using two-dimensional images and three-dimensional statues viewed in virtual reality.

Unlike the two-dimensional studies, which showed no significant differences in viewer perception, our VR experiment with 47 participants found that upright male statues were rated as more attractive and masculine than those posed in a pronounced contrapposto.

Subsequent research extended our experiment to male body models rather than classical statues. These experiments similarly found that contrapposto reduced perceptions of masculinity and dominance. Using eye-tracking, we also examined where observers directed their attention, although we found no significant differences in gaze between the postures.

Interestingly, our earlier research involving female figures found that contrapposto could enhance perceived attractiveness among both male and female viewers. Further studies showed that the posture attracted greater visual attention and influenced neural processing. The same posture therefore appears to influence perceptions of male and female bodies differently.

We later extended our research to examine whether contrapposto also influences assumptions about male sexual orientation. In our study involving 85 gay and bisexual men from North America, participants were more likely to perceive male figures adopting contrapposto as homosexual. These figures were also judged as less masculine.

Another of our studies involving 120 Japanese observers found a similar association between contrapposto and perceived non-heterosexuality. The findings from both these studies are being reported for the first time in my book, The Psychology of Attractiveness and Aesthetics. In the book, I also explore a separate, more speculative possibility – that Michelangelo may have deliberately used this pose to communicate a subtle meaning about male sexuality, drawing on additional artistic and historical evidence.
How modern brains read an ancient pose

In everyday life, we routinely make quick assessments of others from their body language. Upright and expansive postures are often associated with confidence, strength and social standing, whereas shifting weight onto one leg and tilting the hips can create a more relaxed impression.

Our perceptions of sexual orientation may also involve another process. People develop expectations about how men and women typically stand, move and present themselves, and departures from these expectations can shape assumptions about sexuality.

Previous research on body movement has shown that movements perceived as less typical of a person’s gender can influence our judgments about their sexual orientation. Contrapposto may activate similar associations through the positioning of the hips and shoulders, even in a stationary figure.

Importantly, these impressions reflect socially learned stereotypes about masculinity and sexuality rather than characteristics inherent to heterosexual or non-heterosexual men. Our experiments demonstrate how modern observers interpret these postures, not whether posture accurately reveals sexual orientation or whether people in Renaissance Florence shared the same associations.

David has become such a familiar symbol of masculine perfection that we rarely question what its posture might communicate. Of course, these experimental conditions cannot fully reproduce the experience of standing beneath a towering, five-metre marble statue. Yet our research demonstrates that relatively subtle changes in how a male body is positioned can influence perceptions of masculinity, dominance and sexuality.
