articles.title: How a Pittsburgh-born umpire painted baseball history onto the ball itself
articles.author: Christopher J. Phillips, Professor of History, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: Baseballs are charismatic objects. It is no accident that the narrative spine of novelist Don DeLillo’s magnum opus of 20th-century American life, “Underworld,” involves the ownership of the baseball from the “shot heard ’round the world” – the ninth-inning home run New York Giants slugger Bobby Thomson hit to beat the Brooklyn Dodgers for the 1951 National League pennant. A lot of Americana has been projected onto the surface of a baseball.

But the surface of a baseball is not typically a canvas. The 26 or so square inches of area, created when two pieces of leather are connected with 108 red stitches, are awkward surfaces on which to draw. And most of the time, the only thing people want drawn on baseballs is a signature from an admired player.
But that’s not how George Sosnak saw them.

Born in Pittsburgh in 1924, Sosnak worked as a minor league umpire starting in his 30s, but he became better known as a self-taught artist over the subsequent four decades. Each baseball offered Sosnak at least four spaces to fill with images of players, team insignia or text recounting playing statistics or triumphs, all meticulously rendered in India ink.
An ongoing exhibit at the Westmoreland Museum of American Art features over 60 of the approximately 800 balls he finished painting in his lifetime – he began painting nearly 3,000 balls.

Sosnak’s creations are often colorful, depicting players in action, with facts about them or their games written alongside. Many of the baseballs function as miniature stories, a spherical, secular altarpiece that tells the story of a key game or season.
His “Pittsburgh Pirates, 1978” ball features Harold “Pie” Traynor, Bill Mazeroski and Roberto Clemente.

Traynor and Clemente had both died in 1972, the year Mazeroski retired, and the three never played on a single team together. Depicting three of Sosnak’s most legendary hometown Pirates together created a kind of pantheon, with the timeless image of Clemente finishing his swing juxtaposed with the specific moment Mazeroski raised his hat while circling the bases after hitting the home run that won the 1960 World Series.

Sosnak’s scenes often involve these juxtapositions, using the raised seams and the uneven leather strips to both separate and connect moments for artistic effect. He even depicted something other than baseball itself on the balls, including other sports. But his main focus was on using the spherical leather canvas to memorialize the moments and people that mattered to Sosnak – and to fellow fans who commissioned the balls. He often used such detail – spectators in Forbes Field represented by tiny ink dashes – that magnifying glasses are required to fully appreciate the nuances.

Sosnak linked the American folk art tradition with the talismanic nature of an actual baseball. Unlike the case in most other professional sports, some fans come away from baseball games with balls as souvenirs — whether they were hit as home runs or foul balls, or just tossed into the crowd by players.

Baseballs are disposable – most balls last only a few pitches, so around 100 balls are used in every professional game – and yet they become treasured relics when caught. Sosnak’s painted balls combine these tensions: You can hold one in your hand, visualizing its past while touching the otherwise disposable object that was imparted meaning only through the triumph.

articles.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother: the sacred and profane collide in this off-kilter hitman drama
articles.author: Laura O'Flanagan, PhD Candidate, School of English, Dublin City University
paras: A grieving widower with three children and a dwindling supply of frozen breast milk is an unlikely premise for a crime thriller. Yet this is where Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother begins, moving between the intimate demands of fatherhood and a criminal underworld populated by characters who might have stepped from the pages of a comic book.
Director Bassam Tariq’s latest film has moments of domestic tenderness sitting alongside brutal violence, with strange flashes of black humour emerging in the most unexpected places.

Mahershala Ali plays Latif, a devout Muslim and hitman struggling to raise his three children following the death of his wife. In their cramped Texas flat, teenage daughter Fatiha (Adia), eight-year-old Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) and baby Aziza are adjusting to life without their mother. Heartbreakingly, the supply of his late wife’s frozen breast milk is running out, and the baby cannot tolerate formula. This affecting detail highlights the mother’s absence in the daily routines of a household still dependent upon her.

Ali brings an effortless gravity to Latif. Physically imposing yet remarkably still, he conveys a man weighed down by guilt and the responsibilities of fatherhood. There is an economy to his movements which lends poignancy to even the smallest domestic encounters. His capacity for violence appears incongruous with this quiet presence, until he is drawn back into the work he knows.

Crime boss Mike (Laith Nakli) orders Latif to kill Pastor Hwan (John Cho), a former Marine leading a heavily armed group of Christian fundamentalists. Hwan has threatened Mike’s nephew Hatty (Abubakr Ali), who runs a pornography and sex work operation. These figures are grotesque and absurd, verging on caricature, sometimes provoking uneasy laughter with their excesses.

At the heart of the film is Adia’s compelling performance as Fatiha. On the cusp of adulthood, she is beginning to test the boundaries of her independence, even as her mother’s absence places increasing demands upon her at home. The pull of a life beyond the family competes with the needs of her younger siblings. Adia’s emotional intensity gives these domestic tensions a rawness which feels entirely authentic.

The film frequently draws the sacred and profane together in provocative imagery. Latif’s Muslim faith is deeply held, shaping his daily rituals and sense of moral responsibility, though his work as a hired killer presents an uncomfortable contradiction.

His choice of a sword over a gun adds an almost surreal quality to the violence, particularly against the film’s contemporary setting. Pastor Hwan offers a more twisted, fanatical expression of religious belief, using his Christian fundamentalism to justify brutality.

Tariq had originally planned to work with Ali on Marvel’s Blade which was cancelled during development. Certainly, Ali’s acrobatic and inventive sword work in the fight scenes wouldn’t have looked out of place in Marvel’s scrapped vampire-slayer movie. These big fight scenes can jar when juxtaposed with tender moments, but Ali has the presence to pull it off with aplomb, creating an oddly unsettling atmosphere.

Tariq’s cinematography and soundtrack add to this disquiet. Inverted views of the city render familiar streets strange, while the soundtrack occasionally evokes religious chanting. These unexpected flourishes add to the film’s peculiar, off-kilter sensibility.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother occasionally feels uneven. The tonal shifts between domestic realism and outlandish violence are not always comfortably resolved. Tariq’s appetite for the grotesque sometimes threatens to overwhelm the more affecting family drama, though there is much to admire in the film’s refusal to shy away from its own peculiarities.

It is in the relationships between Latif and his children, and the bonds that hold them together in their mother’s absence, that the film finds its greatest strength. There is bloodshed and violence aplenty, but who would have thought the hardest thing to watch would be a little spilled breast milk.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 lets players respawn – a new prison art exhibition shows what happens when you can’t
articles.author: James McLean, Lecturer in Media Production, Graphic Design, and Media Studies, University of Hull
paras: When Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA), the latest entry in the best-selling video game franchise, was announced, UK workers reportedly booked off 83,000 days of annual leave just to be among the first to step into its criminal underworld.

Players hijack cars, orchestrate heists and outrun the law – knowing that if things go wrong, they simply respawn. Yet in the real world, many of the offences that drive GTA’s missions account for over 80,000 immediate custodial sentences a year across England and Wales, where there is no reset button.

This widening gap between the thrill of fictional crime and the grim reality of confinement sits at the heart of our latest collaboration between the University of Hull and HMP Hull. As researchers and prison educators working together on the project, we wanted to explore how creative arts can challenge media stereotypes of crime while supporting prisoner wellbeing – work we have also captured in a short documentary about the collaboration.

The free ACCT Exhibition, which is displayed in the university’s art gallery, challenges media representations of crime, justice and injustice. Using artwork and poetry, prisoners have creatively responded to University of Hull research on confinement, control and surveillance.

The exhibition’s full title, Artistic Comments on Carceral Thematics, is a play on the use of the acronym ACCT (Assessment, Care in Custody and Teamwork). This is a vital process in prisons in England and Wales that monitors and supports the mental wellbeing of prisoners – specifically those at serious risk of self-harm and suicide.
The artists serving at HMP Hull named the exhibition in this way to demonstrate how the creative arts can help people serving sentences to cope with life inside.

In 2026, in the art classroom at HMP Hull, a young man on remand awaiting sentencing worked on his first ever piece of artwork. His paintings were representations of his experience, from crime to prison in the style of GTA’s graphics.

He created these paintings having spoken with one of our team, James McLean, who was interested in the glamorisation of crime through video games. This young artist felt comfortable painting these images because for him, GTA’s world was his world.

Four large-scale paintings based around the game HMP Hull feature in the wider exhibition. Working in collaboration with his teacher, the artist was interested in shifting the accepted narrative of receiving rewards for completing crime-related missions. The paintings in this part of the exhibition show the realities and consequences of such a lifestyle. Accompanying the paintings on the gallery wall is a written explanation of the work:

Even though we have captured the vibrancy and the energy of the game and the “glamourous” life of crime in our work, we have also inserted the moral implications into the story. We have endeavoured to show the reality and the grim conclusion to such a life.

While research shows that playing violent video games is not associated with aggressive behaviour, GTA, like other representations of crime, can potentially glamourise wealth, power and apparent invincibility. This mirrors some real-world drivers of criminal behaviour, particularly motivations rooted in consumer culture and a desire for status and belonging.

True crime, meanwhile, frequently glamourises the way people come to find themselves serving a prison sentence. Researchers have noted that audiences often side with the offender – so long as they are charismatic. Indeed, numerous TV and film hits have centred on offenders, such as Tommy Shelby of Peaky Blinders, Tony Soprano of The Sopranos or Vito Corleone of The Godfather.

But many prisoners have themselves been victims of emotional, physical and sexual abuse during childhood among other adverse childhood experiences. And a high proportion of the prison population have mental health illnesses in comparison to the general population. Because so many people enter prison carrying trauma and poor mental health, finding ways to support their wellbeing inside is critical.

The ACCT Exhibition has created an opportunity to open up conversations about systems of control and coercion that remain unfamiliar to many people. It also highlights the potential of creative practice to support the wellbeing of people serving prison sentences through meaningful activity.

By replacing the fantasy of a quick respawn with the reality of confinement, these artists are proving that while there is no reset button in the criminal justice system, there is still room to rewrite the ending.
The ACCT Exhibition is on display at the University of Hull Art Gallery until December 31 2026

articles.title: The rotters of Rutshire, the Bloomsbury set and loving Lorca: what to watch, see and read this week
articles.author: Jane Wright, Commissioning Editor, Arts & Culture, The Conversation
paras: I’m really enjoying the fact that most people I know who watch Rivals have dropped the “just my guilty pleasure” shtick and now simply confess to full-on loving it.

My own residual guilt stems from the fact that when I was a teenager, my mother, who grew up reading Austen, Dickens and the Brontës, was profoundly disappointed and filled with sorrow to catch me with well-thumbed copies of Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire nonsense. But they were so funny and rude, and also I was horse-mad and a member of the local pony club, so it all just seemed such a good fit. I even went to a fancy ball once in a glittery sequinned boob-tube and thought I was the height of sophistication. Well, it was the 1980s.

Part two of season two picks up after a particularly dramatic part one cliffhanger. Spoiler alert! After discovering the latest affair of her husband Tony (a gloriously nasty David Tennant), long-suffering wife and all-round good egg Monica (Claire Rushbrook) sweeps out of the house in a storm, buckled with grief and humiliation. She somehow finds her windblown way to the house of Lizzie (Katherine Parkinson), also wife to a faithless husband, James (the marvellous Oliver Chris giving hilarious half-Partridge-half-Madeley vibes). The two sit down for a comforting cup of tea, and quickly graduate to the brandy bottle.

But then something extraordinary happens. After her King Lear moment in the storm, Monica is spent and becalmed, and the two women begin to examine the symmetry of their lives with ghastly men who take them for granted. In this scene, says our reviewer Claudine van Hensbergen, the “two frumpiest and most downtrodden women in Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire become the beating heart of the episode – perhaps the whole series”.

It’s Rivals as domestic tragedy, a moment of liberation for two women who realise they would not wish their lives for their own daughters. This poignant scene is the catalyst for change as two worn-down housewives become heroines.
From Moomins to Bloomsbury

The recent release of The Hobbit illustrated by Tove Jansson marks the first time a full edition of the Finn’s Tolkien illustrations has appeared in English. Of course Jansson is best known for the Moomin tales which she both wrote and illustrated.

But anyone familiar with her early illustrations will understand how perfectly her style lent itself to Tolkien’s elvish epic. The imaginations of both Tolkien and Jansson were fundamentally shaped by Finnish myth and folklore, and there are many similarities between the rendering of her own Moomins and Tolkien’s Hobbit characters.

The originality of painters Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant – central figures of the Bloomsbury set – is often sensationalised, with most focus directed on their unconventional sex lives as much as their modernist art. Now a new show at London’s Tate, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury attempts to redress the balance and turn that focus back on the art of this fascinating couple.
On show are more than 300 works that trace the couple’s 50-year creative partnership and visitors can enjoy a full restaging of their studio from Charleston, their exquisite house in Sussex.
Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant Inside Bloomsbury is on at Tate Britain, London till 11 April 2027.

I am so looking forward to watching Spanish film La Bola Negra (The Black Ball). The title comes from the last unfinished play of Federico García Lorca, considered Spain’s most influential 20th-century poet and playwright. This luminous talent was snuffed out when Lorca was executed by firing squad in 1936 at the start of the Spanish civil war, after being imprisoned for his politics and his homosexuality.

Lorca’s unfinished text is a seed that grows and expands into the 21st century, marking three moments in Spain’s history: the second republic in 1932, the civil war in 1937, and contemporary Spain in 2017, taking in three gay stories along the way.
La Bola Negra is in cinemas now.

You Can See Everything is another film I can’t wait to see, which says quite a lot for a three-hour documentary about someone I know very little of. The film has had critics raving as Canadian comedian Nathan Fielder decamps to the house of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of medical company Theranos, in her last days of freedom before she is sent to prison.

Holmes was convicted of fraud after it was discovered that the claims of her blood-testing technology were bogus. Fielder gets literally right in the face of the strange, inscrutable Holmes, who claims she can’t really understand where things went wrong.

In this piece, business academics Kate Kenny and Susi Geiger draw our attention to how gendered stereotypes have shaped Holmes’s story and urge us to interrogate the biases we hold about women like her as we watch the documentary.
You Can See Everything is in cinemas now.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto represented a satirical vision of America – the absurdity of reality has tipped the game into empathy
articles.author: Gaspard Pelurson, Lecturer in Culture, Media and Creative Industries, King's College London
paras: When gaming studio Rockstar announced that its much-delayed new Grand Theft Auto game (GTA VI) would come out in mid-November, most other large scale studios decided to either hold off or push for an earlier release for their titles to avoid being eclipsed.

Growing up, my experience of the universe started with GTA II (1999), its impressive leap to 3D with GTA III (2001), and then Vice City (2002) and San Andreas (2004), which my friends would play during sleepovers. For many players, GTA simply meant sandbox chaos: stealing cars and indulging in gratuitous mayhem.

As I became an adult gamer, I delved lightly into GTA IV (2008) and V (2013), only to realise that the franchise was technically not an American game. Created in Scotland and developed largely by British studios (though today’s massive global teams make it a truly international production), the franchise built its reputation on a distinctly European caricature of the United States: louder, more violent, hyper-capitalist and absurdly unhinged.
Indeed, beneath the violence lay a sharp, progressive satire that the younger audience sometimes missed.
A reality where an alligator is a weapon

Replaying bits of GTA V made this irony impossible to ignore. There are in-game radio ads promoting cigarettes for children, fossil-fuel monopolies funding anti-green energy campaigns and toxic wellness brands peddling self-loathing. It was an exaggerated fun-house mirror held up to American culture; a culture that has since seemed to step through the looking glass.

Over the past decade, following two terms of Donald Trump’s presidency and a steady escalation of political spectacle, the gap between American reality and Rockstar’s satire has shrunk. We exist in a world where a US president openly muses at a press briefing about injecting disinfectant to counter a deadly virus. Then there was the entirely serious state department run by a tech mogul (Elon Musk) named Doge (The US Department of Government Efficiency) – a nod to the his cryptocurrency, dogecoin, which is named after a viral 2013 dog-themed meme.
You have to ask whether the parody has become reality, or whether reality has simply become a parody of itself.

In media theory, the French philosopher Jean Baudrillard coined the term “hyperreal”: a state in which simulations and exaggerated representations become so pervasive that we can no longer distinguish the copy from the original.

Nowhere is this clearer than in the viral side-by-side images comparing GTA VI’s fictional state of Leonida with real-life news footage from Florida. For years, “Florida man” headlines (an internet trope cataloguing the state’s notoriously bizarre, surreal crime blotters, fuelled largely by Florida’s unusually broad public-records laws) have read like rejected GTA mission briefs. For instance, the story of a Florida man who was charged with assault with a deadly weapon in 2016 after tossing a three-and-a-half-foot alligator through a fast-food drive-thru window. That was real life, not a game.
When the real world already operates at maximum absurdity, how do you satirise it?

Early critical consensus around GTA VI points to a striking tonal shift. While players can still cause chaos, if they choose, the game’s narrative pulls in the opposite direction. They are no longer casting players as unhinged sociopaths like GTA V’s Trevor, a volatile, meth-dealing career criminal whose playable storylines leaned into torture, mass rampages and grotesque shock value. Instead, protagonists Jason and Lucia are grounded characters whose ambitions are remarkably modest: surviving, protecting each other and scraping together a decent life.

Critics have even noted how the game subtly nudges players toward empathy, rewarding small, mundane acts of care, like texting a partner, doing a food shop or throwing rubbish in a bin. In this GTA, unprovoked street massacres feel weirdly out of step with the story.

As Rockstar co-studio head Rob Nelson observed in interviews around the release, earlier GTA titles were about the illusion of the American Dream. Today, that dream has shrunk to simply affording a home and looking after your family. In a culture saturated with cynicism, sincerity itself has become the unexpected, almost punk rebellion. It is a bleak take, perhaps, yet also a sign of growth.

This evolution matters far beyond gaming circles. Video games have matured into one of our most revealing cultural barometers. When a blockbuster franchise famous for shock value pivots away from scorched-earth parody toward bittersweet intimacy, it tells us something profound about our current political moment. When reality grows dark and surreal enough on its own, satire no longer needs to be as outrageous.

articles.title: M. John Harrison’s 2026 Booker prize win signals an end for literary snobbery towards science fiction
articles.author: Jon Quayle, Lecturer in Romantic Literature, Newcastle University
paras: M. John Harrison’s 2026 Booker prize win has come as a surprise to many. Not because he didn’t wholly deserve it, but because, at 81, his legacy seemed already settled and secure. He was to be one of the trailblazers for science fiction. Among fans he has been celebrated as an underappreciated writer, who was unfairly ignored by a mainstream literary elite who could not see past tired cliches of aliens and spaceships.

Harrison’s novel, The End of Everything, is not the first winner to draw on the conventions of science fiction. For instance, The Blind Assassin (which won the prize in 2000) by Margaret Atwood includes a pulpy science fiction story embedded within its multi-layered narrative. But Harrison is the first author to come clearly from the world of science fiction and scoop the award. Many readers are hailing the win as the end of snobbery towards the genre.

To appreciate the full arc of this achievement, it’s worth remembering that in the second half of the 20th century and even early 21st, authors like Harrison were struggling to be taken seriously as writers. In fact, science fiction was a genre some writers avoided associating with at all.

In 2009, Atwood, for example, was criticised by science fiction great Ursula K. Le Guin for refusing to categorise novels like Oryx and Crake (2003) as science fiction. “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto,” Le Guin bemoaned. But could she be blamed when other high-profile reviews for that book began with statements like “science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L’”?
There have been fewer limitations on science fiction’s commercial appeal and potential for literary recognition in recent decades.

Science fiction now permeates almost every area of our cultural life, from blockbuster film and TV franchises to video games. On top of this, tech billionaires proudly cite AI films like Blade Runner (the 1982 adaptation of Philip K Dick’s novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?) and Her (2013) as sources of inspiration, seemingly oblivious to the films’ dystopian warnings. But cultural arbiters responsible for fiction awards have been slower to overcome some deep-seated prejudices. So Harrison’s win represents an important nod of acceptance from a literary crowd that once sniffed at the speculative.

Of course, genre snobbery hasn’t always gone one way. The author Carmen Maria Machado describes the relationship between genre fiction and literary or mainstream fiction as an “unending, utterly exhausting fight”, usually taking the form of “tedious cliches” and “petty squabbling”. Perhaps understandably, the more a community feels marginalised, the more it moves to define itself in opposition to the mainstream from which it feels excluded.

In a 1998 article, writer and critic Jonathan Lethem lamented that Thomas Pynchon’s postmodern classic Gravity’s Rainbow was not awarded the 1973 Nebula award – one of the most prestigious awards for science fiction and fantasy. Pynchon’s book plays with ideas of fantastic, speculative technologies and was considered divisive even in literary circles. The Pulitzer advisory board described it as “unreadable”. But had it won the Nebula it would have signalled to the world that artistic aspiration, however divisive, was a key driver of science fiction. For Lethem, its loss marked “the death of the hope that science fiction was about to merge with the mainstream”.

While Lethem was right that resistance from within the science fiction community has also been a barrier to mainstream recognition, his comments inevitably provoke familiar debates about what exactly the “mainstream” is, let alone how to define science fiction. One of the great American novelists, Gene Wolfe, who died in 2019 without his M. John Harrison moment of recognition, argued that science fiction represents literature’s real mainstream:

“When I look back at the foundations of literature, I see literary figures who, if they were alive today, would probably be members of the Science Fiction Writers of America. Homer? He would certain belong to the SFWA. So would Dante, Milton, and Shakespeare. That tradition is literature’s mainstream.”
When future literary historians look back on the genre snobbery of the 20th century, it will hopefully appear as little more than a temporary blip.

Science fiction is a broad church, and there remain plenty of readers who will continue to prefer generic content – representations of the future, encounters with aliens and technological imaginings, for example – over artistic aspiration. The End of Everything is not for everyone, let alone every science fiction reader. But Harrison’s win is a testament to the breadth of the genre and, hopefully, the last nail in the coffin of a snobbery that has unfairly dogged science fiction.

articles.title: US and Iran once practiced diplomacy through archaeology – that legacy need not lie in ruins
articles.author: Kyle Olson, Lecturer in Archaeology, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: When a U.S. airstrike struck Tehran’s Arg Square on March 2, 2026, Golestan Palace was not the target. But it was close enough.

The missile’s impact blew out windows across the palace complex and damaged some of its elaborate 19th-century interiors. In photographs taken afterward, pieces of its celebrated mirrorwork lay scattered across the floor.

Golestan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the great surviving monuments of Iran’s Qajar dynasty, which ruled from 1789 until 1925. Within hours of the strike, UNESCO reported the damage and noted that cultural property is protected under international law during armed conflict.

The palace was not only an early casualty of the U.S.-Iran war, but a symbolically potent one, too. And as my colleague Mehrnoush Soroush at the Center for Ancient Middle Eastern Landscapes has documented, Golestan is not alone. Since the war in Iran began in February 2026, reports of damage to heritage sites have poured in from all across Iran.

I know that damaged buildings — no matter how valuable — cannot compare with the human costs of war. But the images from Golestan have particular resonance to me, an archaeologist who studies the history of relations between Iran and the United States. It also cuts against a history of cooperation between American and Iranian archaeologists, in which Americans worked to preserve, rather than destroy, Iranian heritage.
I have spent years researching how archaeologists, museums and cultural officials from the two countries worked together before the Iranian Revolution of 1979.

My earlier research has examined how archaeology became entangled with American foreign aid and Iranian development programs during the 1960s, and I am currently writing a book on the history of U.S.-Iranian heritage diplomacy over the past century.

I believe that history offers another way of thinking about what has been lost in the current conflict. Long before Iran and the U.S. became adversaries, cultural heritage provided a setting in which people from the two countries learned how to work together.

American archaeologists began excavating in Iran in the early 1930s. In those days, the relationship was unequal: American museums sought access to archaeological sites and, under agreements with the Iranian government, received portions of the objects they excavated under the colonial system of partage. As a result, museums across the U.S. still hold substantial collections of Iranian antiquities.

The terms of the relationship changed considerably during the 1960s, as the U.S. and Iran intensified their connections. At the same time that thousands of American professionals, educators, businesspeople, scholars and others came to work and live in Iran, the country revised its antiquities laws and expanded its own archaeological institutions, universities and museums, resulting in, among other things, a major tourism boom.

American archaeologists still wanted permission to dig at Iranian sites, but they increasingly operated within a system controlled by Iranian officials. In return, American institutions contributed funding and access to laboratories, specialist knowledge, graduate education and connections to an international scholarly community.

American archaeological projects in Iran drew on large networks of such connections. Scholars working on the Deh Luran Plain in southwestern Iran, for example, depended on Iranian government agencies, the U.S. Embassy, American universities and museums, development organizations and scientific laboratories. Botanical remains, animal bones and other materials moved through specialist laboratories abroad, while Iranian officials worked alongside foreign researchers in the field.
Collaboration under the shah

By the 1970s, fieldwork projects were increasingly becoming joint enterprises, based on formal partnerships between institutions and cooperative leadership. Iranian archaeological authorities employed American specialists to help survey areas threatened by dams and other development projects, while Iranian archaeologists increasingly took leading roles in the field. Meanwhile, students moved in greater numbers between Tehran, Chicago, Philadelphia and New York. Museums organized traveling exhibitions, and Iran hosted international scholarly congresses devoted to its history and archaeology.
It can’t be ignored that these collaborations flourished during a period when Iran, under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, was a close American ally.

While the terms of the relationship increasingly favored Iran, they were still marked by geopolitical inequalities. American universities and museums possessed resources that Iranian institutions often lacked – not only financially and in terms of human capital, but physically, in the form of collections of artifacts that had previously been taken out of Iran.
Yet the collaborations also developed lives of their own, as American scholars returned year after year.
Post-revolutionary changes

The Islamic Revolution exposed both how extensive and fragile this network was. Even as the crisis that began in 1978 deepened, American archaeologists did not initially assume that their Iranian partnerships were finished. At Malyan, the remains of ancient Anshan, archaeologist William Sumner proposed continuing to pay a watchman to protect the site, while maintaining contact with Iranian colleagues so research could eventually resume.

That did not come to pass. And much of the American-Iranian archaeological enterprise collapsed as diplomatic relations between the two countries soured after the Islamic Republic took 52 American diplomats and civilians hostage in 1979 and Washington sided with Baghdad during the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s.
But the example of the 1960s and ‘70s points toward a sometimes less visible part of diplomacy: relationships accumulated through repeated practical work.

International relations expert Trita Parsi makes this point in his history of the negotiations that produced the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement. In “Losing an Enemy,” based on interviews with participants on both sides, Parsi describes the working relationship that developed between U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif.

This is not to say that their personal rapport produced the nuclear agreement by itself. Naturally, presidents had to authorize negotiations, diplomats at all levels had to find compromises, and both governments had to conclude that an agreement served their interests. But contemporary reporting described that relationship as one built on professional respect and repeated close proximity. In other words, Kerry and Zarif spent enough time negotiating together to understand each other’s constraints and establish a working relationship despite the hostility between their two governments.

That kind of personal working relationship can assist diplomacy – not just at the highest levels but more broadly across civil society. Sports diplomacy has long been acknowledged; so too the sharing of zoological “gifts.” My research shows that archaeology has long had an important a place in these kinds of cultural exchanges as well.
Today, Iranian conservation specialists are sorting and cataloging shattered fragments from Golestan Palace while attempting to repair damage at heritage sites around the country.

At the same time, American and Iranian officials are still looking for ways to end the conflict. I don’t know what U.S.-Iranian relations will look like when the fighting eventually ends, but damaged buildings and monuments will need to be repaired and conserved. If my inbox is anything to go by, Iranian scholars still want to work together with American colleagues.
And if a larger political opening for U.S.-Iranian rapprochement ever arrives, the relationships built by those who steward and study Iran’s heritage may matter more than they first appear.

articles.title: Eurovision took its song contest to Asia – bringing its political drama and cultural tropes along for the ride
articles.author: Paul David Flood, Assistant Professor of Musicology, University of Tennessee
paras: ABBA and Céline Dion came to the world’s attention thanks to the Eurovision Song Contest, an annual showcase of pop music, camp and spectacle.

Filipino singer Carmelle is hoping that the Eurovision Song Contest Asia will serve as a similar springboard to international fame. On Nov. 14, 2026, Carmelle bested entries from 11 Asian countries to be crowned the Asian edition’s first-ever winner. The competition marked Eurovision’s boldest expansion of its format in its 70-year history.

As a scholar of contemporary European popular music and politics, I study the ways in which Eurovision shapes notions of what it looks like and sounds like to be European. Knowing that the Asian edition would be organized by European broadcasting executives, I wanted to see how closely Eurovision Asia would resemble the flagship Eurovision, or whether it would carve out an identity of its own.

Eurovision’s proposed expansion into Asia dates back to 2008, when the European Broadcasting Union – the transnational coalition of public service media organizations that has organized the Eurovision Song Contest since 1956 – announced plans for “Our Sound – The Asia-Pacific Song Contest.” Originally slated to debut in 2010, the project never materialized.

On March 31, 2026, however, Voxovation, a European-led production company that oversees the development of Eurovision’s spinoffs, announced that Bangkok would host the inaugural Asian competition in partnership with Thailand’s Channel 3 and S2O Productions.
Eurovision Asia is now the second European Broadcasting Union-licensed global spinoff to make the airwaves.
In 2022, Voxovation organized the American Song Contest, which included original songs by artists from all 50 U.S. states, five territories and Washington.

Despite being promoted to the American public in a Super Bowl commercial featuring hosts Kelly Clarkson and Snoop Dogg, the competition failed to attract a large viewership and the spinoff wasn’t renewed.

Given two decades of uncertainty, as well as the failure of Voxovation’s U.S. spinoff, some critics doubted whether the Asian version would succeed. And for a moment, it looked like everything might fall apart: In late October 2026, the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet reported that Eurovision Asia’s original budget of approximately US$4.5 million had been reduced by US$1 million.

The European Broadcasting Union, however, confirmed that the show would go on as planned, and at 8:30 p.m. Bangkok time on Nov. 14, the show’s two hosts, Thai media personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop, welcomed viewers from around the world tuning in via television broadcast and the YouTube livestream.
“Maybe you’ve never heard of Eurovision before, or maybe you’re one of the hardcore Eurofans,” said Bishop. “It doesn’t matter, because you will be blown away by the talent here tonight!”
For the next two-and-a-half hours, each country’s representative performed an original song, with Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên opening the show with her song “Em Tiên” (“Fairy Maiden”).

Vietnam’s entry had many of the spectacular ingredients of an ideal Eurovision entry: bilingual lyrics, large props, flashy outfits and a dance break. The song’s instrumentation included a flute accompanying Tiên’s melody and a bamboo xylophone. It concluded with a second, high-energy dance break reminiscent of electronic dance music genres.

The song’s use of traditional Asian musical signifiers followed the approach of the European entrants that have incorporated folk traditions to promote their national cultures to an international audience.

For example, Ukraine’s 2004 winning entry, Ruslana’s “Wild Dances,” opened with the trembita, a long alpine horn associated with the Hutsul people of the Carpathian Mountains. Armenia’s 2008 entry, Sirusho’s “Qele, Qele,” similarly combined a traditional Armenian duduk flute, zurna trumpet and dhol drums with an upbeat dance track and contemporary pop vocals. While some scholars claim that these musical gestures strategically romanticize and exoticize regional cultures, it’s a way to fuse national identity with modern music.

Other Eurovision Asia entrants also pulled from this playbook. Mongolia’s singer, Beck, wore a deel, the country’s traditional robe, while performing. He also incorporated a traditional Mongolian string instrument into his performance.

Voting, which was open to the general public via an online form, began just before the first performance. Viewers were allotted eight free votes, on the condition that they had to vote for at least three different countries. They could purchase 10 additional votes. The public accounted for half the votes, while a jury made up of representatives from each nation accounted for the other half.

Carmelle’s winning song – a Filipina women’s empowerment anthem titled “Sobra-Sobra” (“Too Much”) – featured a repeated musical line played by a kulintang, a Filipino percussion instrument, and a frenetic dance break. The song’s bridge was rapped in Tagalog, the country’s national language.
As part of her reward, Carmelle will perform “Sobra-Sobra” at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas, Bulgaria.
No Eurovision competition would be complete without a measure of political controversy.

From broadcaster boycotts over Israel’s participation amid the war in Gaza to suspicions that Franco’s Spain rigged the 1968 Eurovision vote in its favor, political disputes have long been part of the competition.

Normally, political statements are not permitted in Eurovision, though exceptions have been made for humanitarian causes. Ukraine’s victory in Eurovision 2022 took place just a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the former Soviet republic. Oleh Psiuk, the frontman of Ukraine’s entrant, Kalush Orchestra, pleaded for support for Ukraine at the end of the performance, which the European Broadcasting Union ended up allowing.
During Eurovision Song Contest Asia, Malaysia found itself at the center of controversy.

Malaysian entrant Aina Abdul, who wears a hijab in her public appearances, performed her song “Bluest Sky.” While Abdul was seen as a possible favorite, Malaysian audiences claimed that she ultimately did not score enough points due to Islamophobia.

Another controversy arose due to the Malaysian broadcaster TV3’s coverage of the show. During the results segment at the end of the show, the camera feed of the Filipino spokesperson, the drag queen Vice Ganda, was cut from the Malaysian broadcast. Malaysian broadcasting laws restrict the airing of drag and LGBTQ+ content on television, radio and digital platforms.
In a comment to The Guardian, Eurovision Director Martin Green said, “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision Song Contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.”
“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation,” Green added.
TV3 has yet to comment on the incident.

Here, there are also echoes of the European competition: Eurovision has embraced multicultural and pro-LGBTQ+ values to such an extent that countries like Hungary and Turkey have withdrawn due to their governments’ incompatible sociopolitical values.
Eurovision Asia’s controversies prove that the European Broadcasting Union has a new – perhaps unexpected – set of geopolitical and sociopolitical values to navigate.

Television viewership for Eurovision Asia varied by market. In Vietnam, the show reached over 5 million viewers. The host country’s broadcast, however, only reached an average of 385,000 Thai viewers. These numbers pale in comparison to Eurovision 2026’s viewership of 131 million viewers across the 35 competing nations.

Nonetheless, hype is already building for the 2027 edition of Eurovision Asia. During a news conference in Bangkok, Voxovation executive Christer Björkman confirmed that multiple cities have expressed interest in hosting, with China, Japan and Taiwan indicating that they’re open to participating in the future.

If more Asian broadcasters buy in, Eurovision will attract an even larger international audience, bringing Voxovation one step closer to turning the contest from a European tradition into a global phenomenon.
But time will tell whether Eurovision Asia can become something more than a European competition staged elsewhere.

articles.title: Oscar Wilde had a surprising rapport with Colorado miners – why it is hard to imagine that happening today
articles.author: Joshua Fagan, PhD Candidate in 19th Century British Literature, University of Washington
paras: Oscar Wilde, the Victorian writer of “The Picture of Dorian Gray” and “The Importance of Being Earnest,” was a fashionable icon known as much for his refined manner and conversation as for his writings.
So the image of Wilde exploring Colorado’s frontier towns and rugged mines sounds like a scene from a dream. But that is exactly what happened during his extensive tour of the U.S. in 1882.
Wilde arrived in the U.S. from Europe with much aplomb. The impresario Richard D’Oyly Carte, the promoter of the acclaimed operetta duo W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, bankrolled Wilde’s tour.

Gilbert and Sullivan had recently written a new comic opera, “Patience,” which mocked the aesthetic movement, of which Wilde was an icon. Championing artifice and refinement in all aspects of life, aesthetes dressed in ornate, unusual ways, such as Wilde’s habit of wearing an unnatural green carnation on his lapel. The often-mocked figure of the dandy, a wealthy man who dressed in the most bizarre and fanciful fashions of day, was an inspiration for aesthetes.

I study 19th-century literature in the English-speaking world, and I see Wilde’s western journey to my home state of Colorado as an example of how intellectual writers in the Victorian era were interested in the working class and how that curiosity was, perhaps surprisingly, mutual.
Wilde’s journey to the ‘Wild West’

Carte brought Wilde to America around the time of the U.S. premiere of “Patience” to help popularize the idea of the aesthete. While on tour, Wilde visited major cities, such as New York and Philadelphia, giving almost 100 interviews. But he also was interested in the “Wild West.” His curiosity may seem paradoxical: Tawdry saloons and dusty main streets were a stark contrast to the atmosphere of luxurious refinement he cultivated.

Yet, above all, Wilde craved the novel and unexpected. He sought experiences and people who were the opposite of the conventionality he saw as chaining Victorian society. The slightly anarchic roughness of the West appealed to him. He called it “the most beautiful part” of the country.

Wilde arrived in Colorado Springs in April 1882. Railroad baron William Jackson Palmer had founded this booming resort town in 1871. The town, a short railway journey from Denver, served as a health retreat for those suffering from tuberculosis – one of the deadliest diseases in the nation at the time.

Befitting its growing popularity, Colorado Springs had a thriving arts scene. According to the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum, “interest in the arts began almost immediately” and was distinguished by the opening of an opera house in 1881. Crafting it in red brick and sandstone, the architects took inspiration from Madison Square Theater in New York. It became one of the most impressive buildings in the state.

Wilde gave his lecture on “The Decorative Arts” at this opera house. He did not condescend to his Colorado audience, nor did he suggest that the highest quality art could only exist in the refined settings of Europe. Instead, he insisted that art should be a part of ordinary existence.

“Art,” he declared, “is not something which you can take or leave” but rather “a necessity of human life.” For Wilde, art meant “value to the workman” and “the pleasure which he must necessarily take in making a beautiful thing.” The quality of art for Wilde was not about luxury and extravagance but about creativity and honesty in creation.

The local paper, The Daily Gazette – now The Gazette – reviewed his talk positively in a column from April 15, 1882. The column praises Wilde for how “the entire evening he commanded the closest attention of his audience.” Reportedly, when he “would give expression to a brilliant thought or idea a murmur of applause would pass through the audience.” The article finishes by exclaiming that the lecture “was instructive and interesting and appreciated by all who were present.”
Wilde’s popularity in the West reveals the oversimplistic nature of the divide between the “highbrow” culture of the literati and the culture of “common” society.

His visit to the isolated, high-elevation mountain town of Leadville makes this blending of “high” and “low” culture even more vital. In this hardscrabble town, which owed its existence to the hard labor of miners, workers came to the Tabor Opera House to hear the lavish aesthete. Similar to his speech in Colorado Springs, he discussed how “beautiful and rational designs are necessary in all work.”
For Wilde, the roughness of his surroundings were closer to his ideal than the conventionality of Eastern U.S. cities, with their “bad wall-papers horribly designed.”
The relationship between Wilde and his Leadville audience was symbiotic. The artist found what he desired in the hard-edged mountain town, far from the pomp and conventions of Europe.
“The revolver was their book of etiquette,” Wilde wrote of the town, not altogether disapprovingly.
He drank with miners, some of whom lowered him into the depths of the Matchless Mine, a riotous atmosphere he found rather exciting.
The miners, he wrote in his “Impressions of America,” were “very charming and not at all rough.” According to Wilde, these miners likewise found value in his discussions about art.
Beyond the ‘highbrow-lowbrow’ divide

Newspaper articles about Wilde’s lectures in Colorado do not emphasize the cultural gap between him and his audiences. That dynamic may not have seemed odd – other than the novelty of a foreign celebrity visiting towns in the interior of the country.

In addition, 19th-century literary culture may not have conceived of the rigid divide between highbrow literati interests and those of the working class that exists today. The historian Lawrence Levine, in his influential 1990 book “Highbrow/Lowbrow,” asserts that supposedly elite pursuits actually had wide appeal in 19th-century American culture.

For instance, opera was not associated primarily with multimillionaires in fancy tuxedos and evening gowns, but was also a popular pastime for all ages and social classes. That opera houses even existed in the frontier towns of Colorado demonstrates Levine’s point.
Working-class residents of Leadville appreciated the chance to hear Wilde lecture about art as much as he relished the chance to travel to a real mining town and talk with its residents.

In my view, economic and cultural divides of today can be bridged so everyone can engage intellectual insights and reflections. Witty, sophisticated authors like Wilde do not simply belong to exclusive elite circles.

articles.title: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors
articles.author: Kate Kenny, Professor of Organization Studies, University of Galway
paras: Despite the countless books, podcasts, TV miniseries and documentaries, people continue to be fascinated by the fall of Elizabeth Holmes and her health-tech startup Theranos. We are now being offered a new insight into the founder through the much-hyped documentary, You Can See Everything.

The initial drama of the documentary takes places 34 days before Holmes started her 11-year prison sentence for investor fraud in 2023. In our research, we examined how Holmes was presented across promotional materials, tweets, talks and interviews over the ten year period from her initial appearance on the public stage in 2013 to the same period in which the documentary begins.

Valued at around US$9 billion (£7 billion) at its peak in 2014, Theranos claimed to have built a device that could run hundreds of lab tests from just a few drops of blood. Holmes and co-founder Sunny Balwani hid that the device could not in fact do what they said, leading to its 2018 shutdown and their convictions for investor fraud (and, in Balwani’s case, defrauding patients as well).

For many, the fascination in Holmes’s story lies in the hubris and deception of this young woman who set out to upend the multi-billion dollar diagnostic industry. But popular perspectives on Holmes obscure something important about how we view entrepreneurs, who we celebrate (or vilify) and whose interests this serves. This is something our research explores.
A highly sellable female entrepreneur
In our analysis, we found that gendered stereotypes helped create an attractive female narrative around Theranos and Holmes between 2013 and 2015 that served (predominantly male) investor interests.

Holmes was introduced as a very specific kind of woman entrepreneur – confident, ambitious, authoritative. The prominent venture capitalist Tim Draper, who made his name backing companies like Tesla and was an early investor in Theranos, praised what he saw as Holmes’s entrepreneurial instincts in 2014. He said she was the first entrepreneur he know who kept quiet about her business “so that the competition wouldn’t get a chance to start … She had a winner and knew it”.
In 2015, Theranos board member and longtime Holmes supporter former US secretary of state Henry Kissinger talked about her as combining “fierce and single-minded dedication with great charm”.
Much was also made of her looks, with the media often noting she was a “young, blond, and blue-eyed” woman. She was a refreshing change from the usual men the industry pinned all its hopes on.

Holmes did present a highly sellable vision of a new Silicon Valley that welcomed and celebrated female entrepreneurs. In her 2019 book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, tech historian Margaret O’Mara noted that Holmes’s rise coincided with growing public scrutiny of Silicon Valley’s lack of diversity, and the “tech-bro” homogeneity of the early-to-mid 2010s. At the time, the Valley was also beset by high profile gender discrimination cases.
For investors, Holmes was an attractive answer to a media problem the tech industry had and the media coverage of her rise certainly helped counter some of critics of the Valley’s “brotopia”.

But Holmes’s brand of female founder was not totally new and this also served investors. In many articles she was portrayed as the female reincarnation of the stereotypical “tech bro” – a Mark Zuckerberg with a heart or a Steve Jobs with a social consciousness.

Then there was her intentional self styling, which the media played up as symbols central to her status as a female tech-visionary. Holmes’s signature black turtle necks seemed to be a homage to the uniform of Jobs, who regularly wore an Issey Miyake black turtleneck. She was asked about it again and again, admitting in an interview with Glamour that she owned 150 of them.

Holmes’s founder uniform combined with the fact that she had dropped out of university to pursue her vision, like Jobs, Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, gave her many of the recognisable characteristics of a successful tech founder. She was like all these visionaries but with the added bonus of being a woman. This portrayal fed straight into investor interests by making Holmes at once both familiar and novel, helping her company Theranos’s value to climb to unprecedented heights.

However, when things started to turn sour, our research found that much less flattering gendered stereotypes were quickly deployed. These narratives framed Holmes’ downfall as female weakness in order to protect powerful men.
Holmes was vilified, not only as a failed entrepreneur, but also as a seductress who had used specifically female charms to lead competent men astray.

According to Rolling Stone, she “lured” male investors into her fraudulent schemes. Meanwhile, the Evening Standard reported her as having “wooed” the men on her board to do her bidding. Financial journalists described how Holmes “dazzled” normally sober leaders at supermarket chains Walgreens and Safeway who then invested in her scheme.

Holmes’s board of directors – once portrayed as the “most illustrious board in US corporate history” – along with the other powerful men she was seen as having duped could now be presented as innocent victims of malicious female magic.

For investors, this villification of Holmes could help them spin their own narratives in order to preserve public trust in their abilities. They could argue that her monstrous supernatural abilities to bamboozle and manipulate were too strong for them to overcome. In this media framing, the fact that investors appeared not to have conducted basic due diligence before investing hundreds of millions of dollars was neither their fault nor a reflection of their real talent for investment. They were simply good men who wanted to help people but had been fooled by a woman playing on an emotional blind spot. They were credulous rather than gullible.

To be clear, we don’t excuse Holmes or seek to diminish the seriousness of what she did. But her story tells us something interesting about the wider system surrounding tech entrepreneurs, and how we can remain blind to the ways capital interests can fuel – and exploit – popular and idolised archetypes.

You Can See Everything provides a new intimate portrait of Holmes, which will add, change or warp ideas we already have about her. But we also need to turn the focus back onto ourselves and think about the ways in which we idolise or judge people in her position – and the gendered stereotypes we would rather not admit to holding.

articles.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
articles.author: Alex Fisher, Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Leeds
paras: It’s that time of year when Christmas adverts start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

Yet companies are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to produce their ads. Last year proved how quickly that strategy can backfire. In the Netherlands, McDonald’s pulled an AI-generated Christmas ad depicting chaotic holiday mishaps after just three days following fierce backlash over the undisclosed usage.

This kind of omission is now restricted under new EU transparency rules that govern how AI-generated content is labelled. Coca-Cola’s 2025 festive campaign drew similar criticism. The advert featured AI-generated scenery and animals that many viewers found uncanny.

Undeterred, this year brands including Very and Plusnet have pressed ahead with AI productions. Because UK law does not require on-screen disclosure, their use of the technology is often tucked away in separate press releases and trade announcements rather than flagged to viewers. Even so, the UK Advertising Standards Authority prohibits misleading omissions if an advert falsely implies human creation to deceive consumers.

Other brands are more subtle with their AI use. While Royal Mail’s 2025 Christmas ad relied on traditional live-action footage, it recently emerged that the campaign used an AI voiceover to narrate the spot.

Replacing human performers – even behind the microphone – has fuelled growing anxiety among both industry insiders and the general public, echoing the fears that sparked the 2023 Hollywood writers’ and actors’ strikes.
Losing trust in animated ads

This growing scepticism means even traditional animation is no longer safe from scrutiny. Dior’s Christmas short film, for example, has generated suspicions among some viewers. Described as hand-drawn and directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet, with an all-star cast featuring Rihanna and Robert Pattinson, it centres on the fashion designer Christian Dior’s friendship with film star Marlene Dietrich.

Commenters praised its authentic visual appearance, while a behind the scenes page was published on Dior’s website highlighting the actors and design sketches, warding off accusations of AI-generation.

Despite this, some viewers believed that Dior’s advert showed several hallmarks of AI. A telltale sign of AI-generated content is garbled hands and fingers. Some viewers pointed to what they perceived as missing fingers and strange hand transitions in the advert.

In an interview with Variety, Chomet and producer Aton Soumache insisted that the advert was hand-drawn and generative AI was never used. But they have confirmed using a process known as “automated interpolation” to generate intermediate frames as “a very small part of the process” for the “repetitive, mechanical part of animation, not the creative work”. Automated interpolation is a standard digital animation tool that precedes AI, but now often involves its use.

The Dior case is illustrative of how vigilant audiences have become about AI use. Just as the presence of deepfakes risks undermining our trust in all images online, a few undisclosed AI-produced adverts can lead to scepticism of all advertising as viewers hunt for evidence of brands cutting corners rather than hiring creatives.
Even when specific accusations prove unfounded, the broader shift in advertising toward undisclosed generative AI raises deeper ethical and aesthetic questions for the industry as a whole.
AI models are often trained on artists’ work without compensation and threaten to put them out of work – not to mention AI datacentres’ impact on communities and the environment.

There’s also an irony in major brands baulking at the tedious task of getting the details right, and giving a misleading impression of fully human creation. These moral defects can diminish our aesthetic experience of AI adverts.

But putting aside morality, the revelation of AI use renders ads aesthetically worse in another way. Philosophers of art argue that forgeries are worse as artworks because they misrepresent achievement. We usually appreciate what the artist did in creating a work. So when we learn that a painting is not a genuine Vermeer, but a 20th century forgery by Van Meegeren, we judge it differently. (One philosopher even likens this betrayal to sexual infidelity – perhaps a bit much!)

Similarly, when we discover a beautiful, animated Christmas ad was produced with AI, we might lose appreciation for its creative process. The appearance of delicately hand-animated characters is a façade, generated not by artistic imagination but raw computational power. It’s not fraud, but it diminishes the experience.

Using AI to assist in creating complex scenery isn’t easy, and there can be skill to its use – some philosophers liken it to gardening. But it’s not the real process of hand-drawing and animation. To present it as such is a misrepresentation of achievement, imitating a style without the requisite labour behind it.

In response to these quandaries, some brands have taken to detailing the human processes behind their animated Christmas ads. Prada’s campaign emphasises traditional hand-drawn animation, with a separate behind-the-scenes video highlighting its artists. Others have followed suit. Barbour and Thatchers Cider each employed Aardman (producers of Wallace & Gromit) to hand-animate their adverts, while Etsy’s festive campaign is not-so-subtly titled “celebrate being human”. There are also video game studios which have detailed their refusal to use generative AI.

The praise showered on these traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft. A season built on warmth and sincerity cannot be manufactured by an algorithm that has never felt either.

articles.title: The nine best books with yearning protagonists for readers who are pining
articles.author: Sarah Olive, Senior Lecturer in Literature, Aston University
paras: There is nothing like the agonising yet delicious slow burn of wanting someone you cannot have. Yearning is behind many great romance tropes, from the tragedy of “right person, wrong time” to the tension of “will they, won’t they”.
The cultural critic bell hooks saw yearning as a universal human condition, which could range from a “passionate collective longing for peace and justice” to an individual longing for a lover.

Yearning is a tradition that has flourished in English literature since 18th-century romanticism, a movement that celebrated the personal and the emotional. For such bittersweet desire to take root, there must be a significant hurdle that makes togetherness seem unattainable. That obstacle can take many forms: unrequited affection, painful shyness, or forces external to the pair.

In literature, these commonly include social stigma, geographical distance and mortality. Whatever the barrier, both it and the longing between the two characters must endure. Suspended between memory and fantasy, caught between a lost past and an imagined future, yearning should consume vast amounts of time and energy. The author must allow the reader to access the inner workings of the pining protagonist, so we can sit with their ache and share it.
If you are ready to luxuriate in the angst, here are nine books to pine over.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
Five ways to find your personal style outside of trends and algorithms
The ick: the psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you
Should you cut off your friend? How to tell when a friendship needs repair, change or an ending
1. Eugene Onegin by Alexander Pushkin (1833)

Two of the book’s characters experience yearning and rejection: cosmopolitan Onegin and country girl Tatyana. Moreover, both characters get a turn at being the pursuer and the pursued in their taut encounters.
Pushkin wrote in Russian. English-language translations variously convey the book’s historic and contemporary qualities.

But if they smack too much of the 19th-century for you, try Clémentine Beauvais’ young adult reimagining, In Paris with You (2018). It transposes the story to 21st-century France. Like the original, it tells the story through the medium of poetry, rather than prose.
2. Love in the Time of Cholera by Gabriel García Márquez (1985)
García Márquez won the Nobel prize for literature in 1982. But the yearning in this Colombian novel deserves an endurance award of its own.
Rejected by the beautiful, young Fermina Daza, trainee telegraph operator Florentino Ariza nevertheless continues to love her for 51 years, nine months and four days.

This does not, however, prevent him from having an enjoyable sex life over the decades. In depicting this, the book underscores that yearning and sexual desire are not synonymous. It is just one way in which the book offers an ultimately hopeful take on an initially tortuous experience.
3. Bel Canto by Ann Patchett (2001)

Also set in South America, the action of Bel Canto is condensed into a few months rather than half a century. Events feel further compressed as they occur under a single roof, in an embassy full of guests taken hostage by revolutionaries.

The hostages are initially kept in cramped conditions, under the watchful eyes of the guards. Language barriers abound as captives from an array of nations work through a single translator. For these reasons, the relationships smoulder before consummation.

Some of the yearnings arise within the group of hostages, others between hostages and their captors. However, they are not limited to the sexual or romantic. They include longings for freedom, home and the characters’ previously mundane lives.
4. The Gift of Rain by Tan Twan Eng (2007)
Malaysian novelist Tan Twan Eng should earn a triple entry in this list because yearning is a staple of his writing.
The longings in three of his books (The Gift of Rain, The Garden of Evening Mists and The House of Doors) eschew yearning that is narrowly romantic or erotic for something more ambiguous.

The stories are steeped in the complex social and political contexts of their setting in colonial and wartime Malaya. The yearnings are straight and queer, familial and national, and treacherous for the characters in both political and personal ways.
5. The Painted Veil by Somerset Maugham (1925)

Eng’s novel The House of Doors takes inspiration from Somerset Maugham’s life and works. These include The Letter (1926) and The Painted Veil (1925). That book gets its own entry here for its plot of yearning that jumps tracks from the selfish to the selfless, the unworthy to the worthwhile.
That may sound moralistic, but the novel mines many grey areas as young socialite Kitty Fane searches for meaning in her life as a doctor’s wife in cholera-ridden rural China.
There’s also a gorgeous film adaptation from 2006 to enjoy once you’ve read the book.
6. Under the Udala Trees by Chinelo Okparanta (2015)

Yearning is a characteristic strongly associated with queer literature. This is unsurprising given the legal, religious and cultural prohibitions of, and discrimination against, same-sex relationships.

The publication of homoerotic literature in such contexts required that authors finely balance expression and suppression. Building on hooks’ work, literature professor Elleke Boehmer argues that a “rarefied intensity of desire” emerges in repressive contexts.

Under the Udala Trees is set in one such context, the 1960s Nigerian civil war. The protagonist, Ijeoma, pines first for a classmate, then for a customer. Yet arguably her greatest longing is for self-acceptance and her mother’s acceptance of her sexuality.
7. The End of the Affair by Graham Greene (1951)
The heart-wrenching yearning in this novel comes in the aftermath of an ecstatic affair, with writer Maurice still pining for married Sarah Miles.
Maurice assumes Sarah has forsaken him for her dutiful but dull husband, Henry. But the eventual plot twist that follows is sharper than a hairpin bend.

The novel is one of several by Greene with a strong Catholic focus. As such, the lovers’ relationships with God form a second triangle in this book. Ultimately, Maurice discovers his true rival is not Henry, but the Almighty himself, transforming an obsessive tale of earthly adultery into an agonising collision between human desire and divine grace.
8. Wuthering Heights by Emily Brontë (1847)
“Haunt me then … drive me mad! Only do not leave me in this abyss, where I cannot find you!”

Wuthering Heights is a tale of dark, destructive yearning across several generations of the same two families. It is also widely found on school curricula, so film versions abound. These include Emerald Fennell’s 2026 movie released to coincide with Valentine’s day, proving that the novel’s afterlife is as perverse as its plot and characters.

If you’re looking for a barrier to true love rooted more explicitly in the supernatural, Stephanie Meyer’s third novel in the Twilight saga, Eclipse (2007), draws strongly on Brontë’s love-triangle classic.
9. Mr Loverman by Bernadine Evaristo (2013)

This novel is a reminder that you are never too old to yearn. Or perhaps, that age is a spur to acting on your feelings. Mr Loverman vies with Love in a Time of Cholera for endurance but exhibits a lighter, more worldly-wise tone throughout.

It spans greater distances, from Antigua to Hackney. Barrington’s wife suspects he is consumed with extramarital passion. She manages to indict most of their acquaintances, except the real object of his affection. The book is unashamedly humorous and poignant. The BBC adapted it as a mini-series in 2024.
